stories.actor: A man captured with his mother; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
stories.event: A man casually remarked that he and his mother were taken captive and he never stopped watching over her.
stories.turn: His remark was offhand, not formal testimony, though a son cannot normally testify for his mother.
stories.outcome: Rabbi permitted the mother to marry into the priesthood on the basis of his remark.
stories.summary: A man, speaking offhandedly, said that he and his mother had been captured by gentiles and that his thoughts were always on her whether drawing water or gathering wood. The case came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who relied on this incidental remark and allowed her to marry a priest.

stories.actor: Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav
stories.event: He swore that his wife's hand never left his during the gentile occupation of Jerusalem.
stories.turn: The Sages rejected his testimony because a man cannot testify about himself, so his wife was forbidden to him.
stories.outcome: He did not divorce her but gave her a separate house in his courtyard and avoided being alone with her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav, a priest, swore that his wife had never left his side while gentiles occupied Jerusalem. The Sages refused his testimony, since one cannot testify about oneself, and she was forbidden to him. He kept her in a house in his courtyard, arranging that she went in and out only with her sons so they were never alone together.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rabbi Meyasha's family; Rabbi Ami
stories.event: A man deposited seven pearls with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without leaving instructions.
stories.turn: Ownership was disputed between the depositor and the heirs.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the depositor, since Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy and the claimant gave an identifying mark.
stories.summary: A man left seven pearls wrapped in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who died without saying whose they were. The parties went to Rabbi Ami, who ruled for the depositor because he knew Rabbi Meyasha could not afford such gems and the claimant described them.

stories.actor: A depositor and Hasa's heirs; Rav Nahman
stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The goblet's ownership was disputed.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman gave it to the depositor because Hasa was not wealthy and the claimant gave a mark.
stories.summary: A man left a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without saying anything about it. Rav Nahman ruled that it belonged to the depositor, since Hasa was known not to be wealthy and the claimant provided an identifying mark.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rav Dimi's heirs; Rabbi Abba
stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: Ownership of the silk was disputed.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded it to the depositor, since Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant gave a mark.
stories.summary: Someone deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without leaving word about it. Rabbi Abba ruled the silk belonged to the claimant because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant could identify it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Hama, Rabbi Afes and Levi
stories.event: Rabbi Hanina refused to head the yeshiva ahead of the older Rabbi Afes and sat outside, joined by Levi.
stories.turn: Rabbi Afes died and Rabbi Hanina took the head seat, leaving Levi without a study partner.
stories.outcome: Levi went to Babylonia, and Rav, hearing of a limping scholar teaching in Neharde'a, deduced what had happened.
stories.summary: Although appointed head of the yeshiva, Rabbi Hanina bar Hama deferred to Rabbi Afes, who was older, and sat outside; Levi sat with him. When Rabbi Afes died, Rabbi Hanina took his place, and Levi, with no one to study with, left for Babylonia. When Rav was told a great limping man had come to Neharde'a and was teaching, he concluded that Rabbi Afes had died and Rabbi Hanina had taken over.

stories.actor: A man, a woman washing her feet; Rava
stories.event: A man grabbed coins from someone and threw them to a woman, declaring her betrothed.
stories.turn: The coins were stolen.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal ineffective, since the owner is not presumed to have despaired of stolen money.
stories.summary: While a woman was washing her feet, a man snatched some dinars from another person, threw them to her and said she was betrothed to him. Rava ruled that the coins were still the owner's, so the betrothal was void.

stories.actor: A sharecropper; Rava
stories.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field he worked.
stories.turn: The owner had not permitted him to take them.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the onions were stolen, so the betrothal failed.
stories.summary: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions taken from his employer's field. Rava asked who had given him the onions and ruled them stolen property, so the woman was not betrothed.

stories.actor: A brewer and the beer's owner; Rava
stories.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with beer sediment belonging to his client.
stories.turn: The owner found him and asked why he didn't use the better sediment.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that this remark did not count as consent outside teruma, so the betrothal failed.
stories.summary: A brewer used sediment from someone else's date beer to betroth a woman. The owner caught him and asked why he hadn't used the better sediment. Rava ruled that 'go take the better ones' counts as consent only for teruma, so the brewer had no right to the sediment.

stories.actor: Homa, Abaye's widow; Rava; Rava's wife
stories.event: Homa came to Rava's court to claim support and wine from Abaye's estate.
stories.turn: As she gestured, her arm was exposed and her beauty dazzled Rava, who went home aroused.
stories.outcome: Rava's wife learned who had been in court and drove Homa out of Mehoza with a chest lock, accusing her of killing three husbands.
stories.summary: Abaye's widow Homa asked Rava for support and then for wine; Rava doubted Abaye drank wine, but she insisted he gave her large cups and gestured, exposing her arm, which seemed to light up the court. Rava went home and asked his wife for relations. She asked who had been in court, and on hearing it was Homa, she chased Homa out of the city, striking her and saying she had already killed three husbands and would not kill a fourth.

stories.actor: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rava; Rav Nehemya
stories.event: She asked Rav Nehemya to allot her sustenance and wine.
stories.turn: Rav Nehemya considered the local custom.
stories.outcome: He granted wine because Mehoza residents drink wine.
stories.summary: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rava came to Rav Nehemya for support and then for wine. He granted both, noting that the people of Mehoza are accustomed to drinking wine.

stories.actor: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya; Rav Yosef
stories.event: She asked Rav Yosef for sustenance, wine, and then silk garments.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef questioned why she needed silk.
stories.outcome: She answered that it was for appearing before him and his colleagues with dignity.
stories.summary: A widow came to Rav Yosef, who granted her food and wine. When she also asked for silk garments, he asked why, and she replied that they were for him, his friends and his friends' friends, so she would not be shamed before them.

stories.actor: A woman litigant; Rav Beivai bar Abaye; Rav Pappi
stories.event: A woman required to take an oath demanded a document of rights written in advance before swearing in town.
stories.turn: Rav Beivai ordered the document written, and Rav Pappi mocked him for the ruling.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappi rebuked Rav Beivai, calling his statement unfortunate.
stories.summary: A woman was obliged to swear an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court, and her opponent asked that she swear in town, hoping shame would make her confess. She agreed only if the court first wrote her a document of rights, and Rav Beivai ordered it written. Rav Pappi scoffed that he spoke unfortunate words because he came from an unfortunate family.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa, Yehuda bar Mareimar and Abba of Sura
stories.event: Rav Pappa pressed a reluctant Yehuda bar Mareimar to join him at the writing of his son's marriage contract.
stories.turn: Yehuda sat silently, and Abba of Sura, thinking he was angry, wrote all his property into the dowry.
stories.outcome: Yehuda said he disapproved, but told Abba not to retract and become a man who goes back on his word.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa went to the family of Abba of Sura to write the marriage contract for his son, and Yehuda bar Mareimar escorted him but did not want to go in, fearing his presence would pressure the bride's father. Rav Pappa forced him to enter; he sat in silence, and Abba of Sura, assuming he was displeased, signed away everything he owned as dowry. Yehuda said he had not wanted even that, and when Abba offered to retract, Yehuda told him not to make himself someone who goes back on his word.

stories.actor: A divorcee; Shmuel; Rav Dimi bar Yosef
stories.event: A divorcee who did not want to nurse her son came before Shmuel, who sent Rav Dimi to test whether the baby recognized her.
stories.turn: Carried past a row of women, the baby looked joyfully at her while she averted her eyes.
stories.outcome: Rav Dimi told her to look up and take her son.
stories.summary: A divorced woman came before Shmuel, unwilling to nurse her baby. Rav Dimi bar Yosef placed her among a row of women and carried the child past them; the baby gazed happily at her while she looked away. He told her to lift her eyes and take her son, since he clearly knew her.

stories.actor: A dying man and Toviya; Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: A man on his deathbed left his property to Toviya and died.
stories.turn: A Toviya came to claim it, raising the question of whether he was the intended one.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come and receives the property.
stories.summary: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya. After his death a man named Toviya arrived to claim it, and Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya takes it, without worrying that a different Toviya was meant.

stories.actor: Ze'eiri and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: Ze'eiri kept avoiding Rabbi Yohanan's offer of his daughter in marriage.
stories.turn: When Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan across a puddle, Rabbi Yohanan confronted him: our Torah is fit but our daughters are not?
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan argued that lineage in Babylonia was no purer, though the Gemara notes he missed Rabbi Elazar's teaching.
stories.summary: Ze'eiri, a Babylonian, avoided Rabbi Yohanan, who kept urging him to marry his daughter. One day Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan on his shoulders across a puddle, and Rabbi Yohanan asked why he honored their Torah but would not marry their daughters. He argued that families of flawed lineage had remained in Babylonia too.

stories.actor: Ulla and Rav Yehuda
stories.event: Visiting Pumbedita, Ulla saw that Rav Yehuda's grown son was unmarried and asked why.
stories.turn: Rav Yehuda feared flawed lineage, and Ulla answered that no one can be sure of his own ancestry.
stories.outcome: Ulla advised him to pick a family by its silence, the way people in Eretz Yisrael judge which quarreler is of finer lineage.
stories.summary: Ulla visited Rav Yehuda and asked why his grown son Rav Yitzhak had not been married off. Rav Yehuda said he did not know where to find a wife of sound lineage; Ulla replied that none of them really knew their own descent, citing verses about ravished women and depraved ancestors. When Rav Yehuda asked what to do, Ulla told him to look for the family that falls silent first in a quarrel.

stories.actor: A seller of glass beads and a woman; Rav Hama
stories.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string, and he asked if she would be betrothed by it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give, give.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that 'give, give' is meaningless and she was not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man selling glass beads was asked by a woman for a string. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she replied 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that this mocking reply meant nothing, so there was no betrothal.

stories.actor: A man drinking wine and a woman; Rav Hama
stories.event: A woman in a tavern asked a man for a cup of wine, and he asked if she would be betrothed by it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give to drink, give it to me to drink.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled her answer meaningless and she was not betrothed.
stories.summary: A woman asked a man drinking in a shop for a cup of wine, and he asked if she would be betrothed with it. She replied 'Pour, pour me a drink,' and Rav Hama ruled this was no agreement, so she was not betrothed.

stories.actor: A man picking dates and a woman; Rav Zevid
stories.event: A woman asked a man knocking down dates to throw her two, and he asked if she would be betrothed by them.
stories.turn: She answered 'Throw, throw.'
stories.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled the answer meaningless and she was not betrothed.
stories.summary: A woman asked a man in a date palm to throw her two dates. He asked whether she would then be betrothed to him, and she said 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that such a reply is nothing, so there was no betrothal.

stories.actor: Two pious men, perhaps Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas
stories.event: One fed the waiter before the meal and the other after.
stories.turn: Elijah's regard differed between them.
stories.outcome: Elijah spoke with the one who fed the waiter first, but not with the other.
stories.summary: Two pious men, said to be Rav Hisda's sons Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas, differed in when they fed the waiter: one before the meal, one after. Elijah the prophet spoke with the one who fed him first and did not speak with the other.

stories.actor: Rav Ashi, Mar Zutra and the king's butler
stories.event: Seeing Mar Zutra grow pale with craving, Rav Ashi put some of the king's food into his mouth.
stories.turn: The butler accused him of spoiling the king's meal, and Rav Ashi claimed the meat was defective.
stories.outcome: On his pointing, leprosy was found in the meat; he told the Sages he had seen a leprous spirit over it.
stories.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat at King Izgur's gate as the chief butler passed with food. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra blanch with craving and put some in his mouth with his finger; when accused of spoiling the king's meal, he said the meat was unfit. Nothing was found until he pointed to a spot, where leprosy turned up, and he explained to the Sages that he had seen a spirit of leprosy hovering over it.

stories.actor: A Roman and a woman
stories.event: A Roman whose proposal was refused ate pomegranates in front of the woman until her craving made her ill.
stories.turn: He offered to cure her if she would marry him, and she agreed.
stories.outcome: He ate pomegranates before her again, had her spit out the saliva, and she was cured.
stories.summary: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she refused. He peeled and ate pomegranates in front of her without sharing, and she swallowed her saliva until she became ill. When he asked whether she would marry him if he cured her, she said yes; he ate pomegranates again and told her to spit, and after something like a green leaf came out she recovered.

stories.actor: A steward of orphans; Abaye
stories.event: A deceased man had used a field as a boundary marker for another's land, then contested it, and his steward pursued the claim before Abaye.
stories.turn: Abaye ruled the claim lost, but the steward argued step by step what the father would have claimed.
stories.outcome: Abaye accepted his arguments and praised him as the kind of steward one should appoint for orphans.
stories.summary: A man had cited a field as a boundary marker attributing it to someone else, later contested it, and died, leaving a steward over his orphans. Abaye ruled that the claim was forfeited, but the steward argued that the father would have said he meant only one furrow, and then that he had bought that furrow back, and Abaye accepted both arguments. Abaye remarked that anyone appointing a steward should choose someone like this, who knows how to argue for orphans.

stories.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin; Rabbi Ami
stories.event: They bought a maidservant for copper coins they did not have, leaving a piece of silver as collateral.
stories.turn: Her price rose and the sellers wanted to cancel.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled no acquisition had taken place, since neither coins nor collateral transfer ownership.
stories.summary: Rav Huna bar Avin's sons bought a maidservant for copper perutot but, lacking the cash, left a piece of silver as security. When her value went up, the sellers sought to back out, and Rabbi Ami ruled that neither the unpaid coins nor the collateral had completed the sale.

stories.actor: Rav Amram the Pious
stories.event: Redeemed captive women lodged in Rav Amram's attic, and one's beauty drove him to lift a heavy ladder and climb toward them.
stories.turn: Halfway up he braced himself and shouted 'Fire in Amram's house!'
stories.outcome: He told the embarrassed Sages it was better to be shamed now than in the next world, and forced his evil inclination out of him as a pillar of fire.
stories.summary: Captive women brought to Neharde'a were lodged in Rav Amram's upper room with the ladder removed. When one passed the opening, her beauty overcame him; he lifted a ladder ten men could not carry and began to climb. Halfway he stopped himself and cried 'Fire in Amram's house!'; when the Sages complained he had shamed them, he said shame in this world was better than in the next, then made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire.

stories.actor: Rabbi Meir
stories.event: Rabbi Meir, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan appear as a woman across a river and began crossing a rope bridge to her.
stories.turn: Halfway across, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said that only heaven's warning about Rabbi Meir kept him from ruining him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman on the far side of a river, and with no ferry he started across a rope bridge. Halfway, Satan let go and told him that only the heavenly proclamation to beware of Rabbi Meir and his Torah had saved him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva
stories.event: Rabbi Akiva, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan appear as a woman atop a palm tree and began climbing.
stories.turn: Halfway up, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning about Rabbi Akiva kept him from ruining him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also scoffed at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and he began to climb. Halfway, Satan left him and said that only heaven's warning to beware of Rabbi Akiva had protected him.

stories.actor: Peleimu
stories.event: Peleimu, who daily mocked Satan, was visited on Yom Kippur eve by Satan disguised as a pauper.
stories.turn: The pauper demanded to come in and sit at the table, then behaved repulsively.
stories.outcome: The story is cut off as Peleimu begins to rebuke him.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to say every day 'An arrow in Satan's eye.' On the eve of Yom Kippur, Satan came to his door as a poor man; Peleimu gave him bread, then brought him in and seated him at the table at his insistence. Covered in boils, the guest behaved disgustingly, and Peleimu began to speak to him as the window ends.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel
stories.event: Funeral costs had become so heavy that families abandoned their dead.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in plain linen garments.
stories.outcome: Everyone followed his example, and burial in simple garments became the custom.
stories.summary: Burials had grown so lavish that the expense was harder on families than the death itself, and some fled leaving the dead unburied. Rabban Gamliel instructed that he be buried in plain linen, and the whole people followed his lead.

stories.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon; the Sages
stories.event: The Sages awarded her four hundred gold coins a day for perfumes from her late husband's estate.
stories.turn: She responded by blessing them.
stories.outcome: She wished the same for their daughters, and they answered Amen.
stories.summary: When the Sages allotted Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter four hundred gold coins for one day's perfume, she told them to provide this way for their own daughters, and they answered Amen.

stories.actor: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
stories.event: Leaving Jerusalem, he saw a girl picking barley from Arabs' animal dung, who asked him for support.
stories.turn: She revealed she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, whose marriage contract he had signed for a million gold dinars.
stories.outcome: He wept and lamented that when Israel does not do God's will it is delivered even to the animals of a lowly nation.
stories.summary: Riding out of Jerusalem with his students, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw a young woman gathering barley from the dung of Arabs' animals; she covered herself with her hair and begged him for food. She said she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, that her family's wealth was lost, and reminded him he had signed her marriage contract. He recalled the enormous dowry, wept, and said Israel's fate depends on doing God's will.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: He saw Nakdimon's daughter gathering barley from between horses' hooves in Akko.
stories.turn: Moved by the sight, he applied a verse to her.
stories.outcome: He read the Song of Songs verse as 'feed your bodies' about her plight.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok swore he had seen Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter gathering barley between horses' hooves in Akko. He recited a verse from Song of Songs about her, rereading 'your kids' as 'your bodies.'

stories.actor: A blind man, a messenger and Mar Shmuel
stories.event: Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to fetch a late blind student, but they missed each other.
stories.turn: The messenger reported that he had seen the blind man's wife committing adultery.
stories.outcome: Mar Shmuel told the blind man to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not otherwise.
stories.summary: A blind man who recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel was late one day, so Shmuel sent a messenger, who went one way while the blind man came another. The messenger returned saying the man's wife had committed adultery. When the blind man asked Shmuel, he was told to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not if he didn't.

stories.actor: King Yannai, Elazar ben Po'ira and the Sages
stories.event: Celebrating a victory, Yannai feasted the Sages, and Elazar ben Po'ira claimed they secretly opposed him.
stories.turn: When Yannai wore the frontplate, the elder Yehuda ben Gedidya told him to give up the priesthood, citing a rumor about his mother that proved false.
stories.outcome: Urged by Elazar, Yannai had the Sages killed, and Torah was desolate until Shimon ben Shatah restored it.
stories.summary: After conquering sixty cities, King Yannai held a feast for the Sages, where the scoundrel Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees resented him and suggested testing them with the priestly frontplate. The elder Yehuda ben Gedidya told Yannai to be content with the crown and leave the priesthood, because of a rumor that his mother had been captured; the rumor was investigated and found baseless, and the Sages were expelled in anger. Elazar then urged Yannai to destroy them, saying the Torah lay in a corner for anyone to study, and all the Sages were killed until Shimon ben Shatah restored the Torah.

stories.actor: A Jew and a gentile traveling together
stories.event: A gentile who could not keep pace with a Jew reminded him of the Temple's destruction to slow him.
stories.turn: The Jew groaned but kept walking fast, and the gentile asked why groaning had not weakened him.
stories.outcome: The Jew explained that a grief long familiar no longer breaks a person.
stories.summary: A gentile walking with a Jew could not keep up, so he mentioned the destruction of the Temple to sadden him. The Jew sighed but still outpaced him, and when the gentile asked why the sigh hadn't broken him, he said that only a new sorrow does that, not one people are used to.

stories.actor: Rabbi Abbahu
stories.event: Rabbi Abbahu, supported by two slaves in a bathhouse, was caught when it collapsed.
stories.turn: He grabbed a pillar and climbed out.
stories.outcome: He pulled both slaves up with him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Abbahu was standing in a bathhouse, held up by two slaves, when it collapsed beneath him. He caught hold of a pillar, climbed up, and lifted both slaves to safety.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: Climbing stairs supported by Rav Ami and Rav Asi, Rabbi Yohanan felt the stair collapse.
stories.turn: He climbed up and lifted both of them, prompting the Sages to ask why he needed support.
stories.outcome: He replied that he was saving his strength for old age.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan was going up stairs with Rav Ami and Rav Asi supporting him when a step gave way. He went up and pulled them both up with him. When the Sages asked why so strong a man needed support, he said he was saving his strength for old age.

stories.actor: Abaye and Rav Mesharshiyya
stories.event: Abaye rode along the Sagya River while Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis sat on the far bank and did not stand for him.
stories.turn: Abaye challenged them, asking whether he was not their primary teacher.
stories.outcome: They answered that they had not noticed him.
stories.summary: Abaye was riding a donkey along the bank of the Sagya River, and Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis sitting on the opposite bank did not rise for him. He asked them whether he was not their primary teacher, to whom they owed that honor even at a distance. They told him it had not entered their minds; they had not seen him.

stories.actor: Ravina and Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
stories.event: While Ravina sat before Rabbi Yirmeya, a man passed by without covering his head.
stories.turn: Ravina called the man rude.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yirmeya excused him as probably coming from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are so common people are less careful.
stories.summary: Ravina was sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti when a man walked past without covering his head. Ravina remarked how rude the man was. Rabbi Yirmeya suggested he was probably from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are common and people do not take such care.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Rabbi Elazar moved to Eretz Yisrael, was ordained, and was appointed to the council that intercalates the calendar.
stories.turn: At each step he declared he had been spared one more of the three curses Ezekiel pronounces on false prophets.
stories.outcome: He had been spared all three.
stories.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse; when he was ordained, two; and when he was seated on the council for intercalating the calendar, three. The curses come from Ezekiel 13:9: being excluded from the council of God's people, from the register of Israel, and from the land of Israel.

stories.actor: Rabbi Zeira and a Sadducee
stories.event: On his way to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Zeira found no ferry and crossed the Jordan holding a rope.
stories.turn: A Sadducee mocked the Jews as a hasty people who still had not changed.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Zeira answered that he hurried because even Moses and Aaron had not merited entering the land, so he could not be sure he would.
stories.summary: Rabbi Zeira could not find a ferry across the Jordan, so he pulled himself across on a rope. A Sadducee taunted him: the Jews had said 'we will do' before 'we will hear' and were still hasty. Rabbi Zeira replied that Moses and Aaron had not merited entering this land, so who was to say he would, and he would not wait.

stories.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of Bar Elyashiv
stories.event: She sued the orphans for her marriage-contract payment and was taking them to court.
stories.turn: The orphans said it embarrassed them that she went in house clothes, so she put on all her clothes, and the clothes she wore became part of the case.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled with Rav that a widow's clothes on her body are appraised and counted against her payment.
stories.summary: A widow in the Bar Elyashiv family was taking the orphans to court over her marriage contract. They told her it shamed them for her to go dressed as she was, so she dressed in and wrapped herself with all her clothing. Before Ravina, he ruled according to Rav that the clothes a widow is wearing are appraised, so everything she had put on was counted toward her settlement.

stories.actor: Shmuel's father, Shmuel, and Shmuel's daughters
stories.event: Shmuel's father posted guards over captive women brought to Neharde'a, and Shmuel questioned the point, since no one had guarded them before.
stories.turn: His father asked whether he would treat them so if they were his own daughters, and later Shmuel's daughters were in fact taken captive and brought to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.outcome: The daughters declared themselves pure before their captors entered and were permitted to marry priests; they turned out to be Shmuel's daughters, and Rabbi Hanina told the priest Rav Shemen bar Abba to marry one of them.
stories.summary: Shmuel's father put guards on captive women in Neharde'a, and when Shmuel asked who had guarded them until then, his father asked whether he would show such contempt if they were his daughters. The words came true: Shmuel's daughters were captured and taken to Eretz Yisrael. They left their captors outside, went into Rabbi Hanina's study hall, each said 'I was captured and I am pure', and were permitted to marry priests before the captors came in. Rabbi Hanina saw they were daughters of great scholars, which proved to be so, and he told Rav Shemen bar Abba to go and marry one of his relatives, brushing off his worry about witnesses abroad.

stories.actor: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
stories.event: The impoverished woman reminded Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai that he had signed her marriage contract.
stories.turn: He recalled that it listed a dowry of a million gold dinars.
stories.outcome: He wept and said that when Israel does not do God's will it is handed over even to the animals of a lowly nation.
stories.summary: The destitute woman asked Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai whether he remembered signing her marriage contract. He told his students that he had, and that it listed a million gold dinars from her father's house alone. He wept and said that when Israel does God's will no nation rules it, and when it does not, it is handed over to a lowly nation and even to that nation's animals.

stories.actor: Abaye and his tenant farmer
stories.event: Abaye's tenant farmer asked whether he could betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months, and Abaye permitted it.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef told Abaye that Rav and Shmuel require twenty-four months; Abaye ran parasangs after the tenant but could not catch him.
stories.outcome: Abaye concluded that one should not rule even on a simple matter in his teacher's vicinity, because he will not succeed in getting it right.
stories.summary: Abaye's tenant farmer asked whether he could betroth a nursing woman fifteen months after the birth, and Abaye said yes, giving several reasons. When Abaye told Rav Yosef, he learned that Rav and Shmuel require a twenty-four-month wait. Abaye ran three parasangs after the tenant (some say one through sand) but did not catch him. He took the lesson that one should not rule in one's teacher's vicinity, since even knowing the law he had failed to say it correctly.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: They planned to let a woman remarry right away because her child had been given to a wet nurse, as a baraita allows.
stories.turn: An old woman said Rav Nahman had forbidden exactly this in her own case, and Rav Pappi cited Rabbi Meir's decrees against them.
stories.outcome: They admitted they had not had that principle in mind.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua were about to rule by a baraita that a nursing mother whose child is with a wet nurse may remarry at once. An old woman told them Rav Nahman had forbidden this in her own case. Rav Pappi then reminded them of a baraita in which Rabbi Meir requires every woman to wait three months, and of Shmuel's rule that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's decrees. They answered that it had not been in their minds.

stories.actor: Hillel the Elder
stories.event: Hillel provided a poor man of good family with a horse and a servant to run before him.
stories.turn: One time no servant could be found.
stories.outcome: Hillel himself ran before the man for three mil.
stories.summary: Hillel the Elder got a poor man from a distinguished family a horse to ride and a servant to run in front of him, since that was what the man lacked. Once, when Hillel could not find a servant, he ran in front of the man himself for three mil.

stories.actor: Rabbi Nehemya and a poor man
stories.event: A poor man asked Rabbi Nehemya for support and said he usually ate fatty meat and aged wine.
stories.turn: Rabbi Nehemya invited him to share his lentils, and the man ate them and died.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Nehemya said, 'Woe to this one, whom Nehemya killed,' which the Gemara reads as blaming the man for pampering himself so much.
stories.summary: A man asked Rabbi Nehemya for charity, saying he was used to fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya asked whether he would come down to sharing his lentils; the man did, and he died. Rabbi Nehemya's lament, 'woe to this one whom Nehemya killed', is explained as meaning the man should not have indulged himself to that degree.

stories.actor: Rava and a poor man
stories.event: A poor man asked Rava for support and said he dined on fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.turn: When Rava asked whether he cared about burdening the community, the man said God provides for each person; just then Rava's sister, unseen for thirteen years, arrived with a fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.outcome: Rava took it as an answer from Heaven, conceded, and told the man to sit and eat.
stories.summary: A poor man told Rava he was used to fattened hen and aged wine. Rava asked whether he did not worry about the strain on the community, and the man answered that he ate from God's provision, citing 'You give them their food in its time'. At that moment Rava's sister, whom he had not seen in thirteen years, arrived bringing a fattened hen and aged wine. Rava told the man that he gave in to him, and invited him to eat.

stories.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon and the Sages
stories.event: The Sages awarded her four hundred gold coins for perfumes for a single day from her late husband's estate.
stories.turn: She told them they should award the same to their own daughters.
stories.outcome: They answered after her, 'Amen'.
stories.summary: When the Sages set an allowance of four hundred gold coins for one day's perfume for Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, she said to them: this is how you should pledge for your own daughters. They responded, 'Amen'.

stories.actor: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
stories.event: Riding out of Jerusalem, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw a young woman picking barley out of Arabs' animals' dung, and she begged him for food.
stories.turn: She was the daughter of the rich Nakdimon ben Guryon, whose family fortune had been lost, and she reminded him he had signed her marriage contract listing a million gold dinars.
stories.outcome: He wept and said that when Israel does not do God's will it is handed over even to the animals of a lowly nation.
stories.summary: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, riding out of Jerusalem with his students, saw a girl gathering barley from animal dung; she covered herself with her hair and asked him to support her. She told him she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter and that her father's money and her father-in-law's had both been lost. She reminded him he had signed her marriage contract, and he recalled that it listed a million gold dinars from her father's house. He wept, saying that when Israel fails to do God's will it is handed over to a lowly nation and even to its beasts.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and his wife
stories.event: Mar Ukva secretly left four dinars every day in a poor neighbor's door socket, and one day the poor man came out to see who it was.
stories.turn: Mar Ukva and his wife fled into a hot furnace, where his feet were burned but hers were not.
stories.outcome: She explained that her charity was greater because she gave food directly from the house, and he understood why she was spared.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to toss four dinars into a poor neighbor's door socket each day. One day the poor man decided to find out who was doing it, and that day Mar Ukva's wife came with him. When the man came out after them, they ran and hid in a furnace that was still hot; Mar Ukva's feet were scorched, and his wife told him to rest them on hers. He was upset, and she told him her charity was worth more because she was at home and gave immediate help in food.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and a poor neighbor
stories.event: Mar Ukva sent four hundred dinars to a poor neighbor every Yom Kippur eve, and one year his son brought it.
stories.turn: The son came back saying the man did not need it, since he had seen old wine being sprinkled for him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva said the man was that pampered, doubled the sum, and sent it.
stories.summary: Each Yom Kippur eve Mar Ukva sent four hundred dinars to a poor man in his neighborhood. One year he sent it with his son, who returned saying the man did not need charity, because he had seen them pouring old wine on the floor for him. Mar Ukva replied that if he was so used to luxury, he needed more, and he doubled the gift.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records.
stories.turn: They showed seven thousand gold dinars, and he judged this too little provision for the long road ahead.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his remaining wealth.
stories.summary: As Mar Ukva was dying, he asked for his charity accounts and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. He said his provisions were light and the road long. He got up and gave away half his money; the Gemara explains that the one-fifth limit on charity does not apply at death.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents and the heirs
stories.event: The heirs of a deceased man claimed a bag of documents deposited with a woman, and she said she had seized it while he was alive.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked whether she had witnesses that the man had demanded it from her in his lifetime and she refused, and she had none.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled it a seizure after death, which is invalid.
stories.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and the depositor's heirs came to claim it. She said she had seized it from him while he was alive. Rav Nahman asked whether she had witnesses that he had asked for it during his life and she had refused. She had none, so he ruled it was a seizure after death, which counts for nothing.

stories.actor: Rava and the daughter of Rav Hisda
stories.event: A woman in Rava's court was obligated to take an oath.
stories.turn: Rav Hisda's daughter, Rava's wife, told him she knew the woman to be suspect of swearing falsely.
stories.outcome: Rava transferred the oath to the opposing party.
stories.summary: A woman was required to take an oath in Rava's court. Rav Hisda's daughter told Rava she knew the woman was suspect about oaths. Rava reversed the oath onto the other side.

stories.actor: Rava, Rav Pappa, and Rav Adda bar Mattana
stories.event: Rav Pappa told Rava he knew a document brought before him had already been paid.
stories.turn: Rava said one witness is nothing, and Rav Adda bar Mattana asked why Rav Pappa should count for less than Rav Hisda's daughter.
stories.outcome: Rava answered that he knew her truthfulness with certainty but not Rav Pappa's.
stories.summary: A document came before Rava while Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana sat with him, and Rav Pappa said he knew it had been paid. Rava asked whether anyone else knew this; when Rav Pappa said no, Rava declared that a single witness is nothing. Rav Adda objected that Rava had relied on Rav Hisda's daughter alone. Rava replied that he was certain of her honesty but not of Rav Pappa's.

stories.actor: Rav Aha bar Abba and Rav Hisda
stories.event: Visiting his son-in-law Rav Hisda, Rav Aha bar Abba sat his granddaughter on his lap.
stories.turn: Rav Hisda objected that she might already be betrothed, and each accused the other of breaking a ruling.
stories.outcome: Rav Aha said he followed Shmuel's other ruling, that everything is permitted when done for the sake of Heaven.
stories.summary: Rav Aha bar Abba came to Rav Hisda's house and put his daughter's daughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether he did not think she might be betrothed; Rav Aha retorted that if so, Rav Hisda had broken Rav's rule against betrothing a minor daughter. Rav Hisda countered that Rav Aha was breaking Shmuel's rule against making use of a woman. Rav Aha answered that he followed another statement of Shmuel: all is for the sake of Heaven.

stories.actor: Mari bar Isak, a man claiming to be his brother, and Rav Hisda
stories.event: A man arrived from Bei Hoza'a claiming to be Mari bar Isak's brother and demanded a share of their father's estate, and Mari said he did not know him.
stories.turn: The claimant said his witnesses were afraid of Mari, who was a violent man, so Rav Hisda shifted the burden of proof onto Mari.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda told Mari that this is how he judges him and all violent men like him.
stories.summary: A man came from Bei Hoza'a to Mari bar Isak saying he was his brother and wanted his share of their father's property. Mari said he did not recognize him, and Rav Hisda first agreed that this was a fair answer, since Joseph too went unrecognized. When the claimant said his witnesses feared the violent Mari, Rav Hisda ordered Mari to bring witnesses that the man was not his brother. Mari protested that the claimant bears the burden of proof, and Rav Hisda replied that this is how he judges Mari and violent men like him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives
stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized a cow belonging to orphans in an alley, and Rabbi Yohanan approved.
stories.turn: Reish Lakish told them to give it back.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan told them he could do nothing, since his equal disagreed with him.
stories.summary: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan seized an orphans' cow to cover a debt, and Rabbi Yohanan told them they had done well. Reish Lakish then told them to go and return it. When they came back to Rabbi Yohanan, he said there was nothing he could do, because a scholar of his own standing disagreed with him.

stories.actor: A herdsman of orphans and a creditor
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, claiming he took it before the debtor died, while the herdsman said it was after.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked the herdsman for witnesses to the seizure, and he had none.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the creditor, since he could have claimed he bought the ox.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman looking after orphans' cattle. The creditor said he seized it in the debtor's lifetime; the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman asked the herdsman whether he had witnesses to the seizure, and he did not, so Rav Nahman ruled that the creditor's word stands, since he could just as well have claimed he had bought it.

stories.actor: The house of the Nasi and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: Members of the Nasi's household seized an orphans' maidservant, and Rabbi Abbahu approved.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abba rebuked the judges for flattering the Nasi's house.
stories.outcome: He reminded them that Reish Lakish had reversed such a ruling made according to Rabbi Tarfon.
stories.summary: The Nasi's household seized a maidservant belonging to orphans in an alley, to cover a debt. Rabbi Abbahu, sitting with Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, said they had done well. Rabbi Abba, sitting with them, asked whether they were flattering the Nasi's house, reminding them that Reish Lakish had overturned exactly such a ruling.

stories.actor: Yeimar bar Hashu and his agent
stories.event: When a debtor of Yeimar bar Hashu died leaving a boat, Yeimar sent his agent, who seized it.
stories.turn: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua met the agent and told him he was seizing for one creditor to the loss of others.
stories.outcome: The window ends as they cite Rabbi Yohanan's ruling against such a seizure.
stories.summary: A man who owed Yeimar bar Hashu money died and left a boat, and Yeimar told his agent to seize it, which he did. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua met the agent and told him he was seizing for one creditor where it harms other creditors. They began citing Rabbi Yohanan's ruling on that case, and the window cuts off there.

stories.actor: Avimi and his father Rabbi Abbahu
stories.event: Rabbi Abbahu asked his son Avimi for water and fell asleep before it arrived.
stories.turn: Avimi stood bent over him until he woke.
stories.outcome: As a reward, Avimi succeeded in expounding the psalm 'A song of Asaph'.
stories.summary: Avimi, who already had five ordained sons, still ran to open the gate for his father Rabbi Abbahu. One day his father asked him for water and dozed off before he brought it. Avimi stood bent over him until he woke, and as a reward he succeeded in expounding Psalm 79.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tarfon
stories.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could step on him to get in and out of bed, and he boasted of this in the study hall.
stories.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached even half of the honor due to her.
stories.outcome: They asked whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea in front of him without his shaming her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would bend down so that his mother could climb onto her bed and step down onto him. He praised himself for this in the study hall. The Sages told him he had not reached half the honor owed: had she ever thrown his purse into the sea before his eyes without his embarrassing her?

stories.actor: Rav Asi and his elderly mother
stories.event: Rav Asi's elderly mother made more and more demands, ending with a husband as handsome as he was, so he left her and went to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: He heard she was following him and asked Rabbi Yohanan whether he could leave the land to meet her.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he did not know, and when Rav Asi returned, saw he was set on going and wished him a safe return.
stories.summary: Rav Asi's aged mother asked for jewelry, which he made her, then for a husband, whom he said he would find, then for a husband as handsome as he. He left her and went to Eretz Yisrael. Hearing she was coming after him, he asked Rabbi Yohanan whether one may leave the land, and was told no; to greet one's mother, Rabbi Yohanan said he did not know. When Rav Asi came back a little later, Rabbi Yohanan said: you are set on leaving; may God bring you back in peace.

stories.actor: A man in Shihin
stories.event: A man inherited three mustard stalks from his father, and one of them broke.
stories.turn: That single stalk turned out to hold nine kav of mustard.
stories.outcome: Its wood was used to roof an artisans' booth.
stories.summary: Rav Yosei reported a case in Shihin: a man's father left him three mustard stalks, and one split open. Nine kav of mustard were found in it. Its wood was big enough to roof a potters' booth.

stories.actor: A man who rented a donkey, and Rava and Abaye
stories.event: A man rented out his donkey with orders not to take the Pekod River road, where there is water, but the renter took that road and the donkey died.
stories.turn: Before Rava the renter admitted taking the road but said there was no water, and Rava accepted this because he could have lied more effectively.
stories.outcome: Abaye objected that this argument does not apply where witnesses establish the facts.
stories.summary: A man rented his donkey to someone and told him to take the dry Neresh road, not the Pekod River road, where there is water. The renter took the river road and the donkey died. Before Rava he admitted using the river road but said it had no water then, and Rava accepted the claim because he could have simply said he took the other road. Abaye countered that this kind of argument does not hold against facts that witnesses know.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
stories.event: Reclining in the upper room of the house of Nit'za in Lod, the Elders were asked whether study or action is greater.
stories.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action and Rabbi Akiva said study.
stories.outcome: All agreed that study is greater, because study leads to action.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were reclining in an upper room in Lod when they were asked whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon answered action, and Rabbi Akiva answered study. In the end they all said study is greater, because it leads to action.

stories.actor: Rav Yehuda, Rav Nahman, and a man from Neharde'a
stories.event: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda in a Pumbedita butcher shop, and Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and proclaimed him a slave.
stories.turn: The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nahman's court; Rav Yehuda corrected Rav Nahman's every word, defended his ruling, and with Rav Mattana's arrival confirmed Shmuel's saying that anyone claiming Hasmonean descent is a slave.
stories.outcome: The man was proclaimed a slave, many marriage contracts in Neharde'a were torn up, and Rav Yehuda stopped a crowd from stoning him by threatening to reveal their lineage, so they dropped their stones and dammed the river.
stories.summary: A man from Neharde'a, told to wait at a Pumbedita butcher shop until Rav Yehuda's servant was served, mocked Rav Yehuda; Rav Yehuda excommunicated him, and since the man called others slaves, he proclaimed him a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda before Rav Nahman, and Rav Yehuda went on Rav Huna's advice. At every courtesy Rav Nahman offered, Rav Yehuda corrected his words and his conduct, until Rav Nahman's wife Yalta urged her husband to finish with him. Rav Nahman heard the case. When the man claimed Hasmonean descent, Rav Yehuda quoted Shmuel that anyone saying so is a slave. Rav Mattana, arriving that day after thirteen years away, confirmed it with the story of the last Hasmonean girl who leapt from a roof. The man was declared a slave and many marriages in Neharde'a were undone. As Rav Yehuda left, the townspeople came to stone him, but he threatened to reveal Shmuel's list of the city's flawed families; they dropped their stones, which formed a dam in the Malka River.

stories.actor: Aher (Elisha ben Avuya)
stories.event: Aher witnessed something that shook his faith.
stories.turn: Some say he saw a son die while fulfilling a mitzva; others, that he saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator dragged in the dirt by a pig.
stories.outcome: He went out and sinned.
stories.summary: The Gemara gives two accounts of what made Elisha ben Avuya, called Aher, abandon the Torah. In one, he saw a son die while performing a mitzva that promises long life. In the other, he saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit being dragged by a pig and cried, 'Shall a mouth that produced pearls lick the dust?' After that he went out and sinned.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, and he covered himself with boils by an incantation, but she healed him by magic.
stories.turn: He fled and hid in a demon-haunted bathhouse where even two people together would be harmed.
stories.outcome: He survived, guarded all night by two of the emperor's armor-bearers, which the Sages explained as a miracle for resisting sin.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. He said a spell that covered him in boils and scabs, but she used magic to heal him. He fled and hid in a bathhouse so dangerous that even two people entering by day were harmed. The next day he told the Sages that two imperial guards had watched over him all night, and they said this miracle came because he had escaped a forbidden sexual temptation.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok, and he asked for food, so she began roasting non-kosher food in her oven.
stories.turn: He climbed into the hot oven and said that whoever does this act falls into this fire.
stories.outcome: She said that had she known it mattered so much to him, she would not have tormented him.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Tzadok. He said he was too weak and asked for something to eat, and she offered non-kosher food, reasoning that one who does the one thing eats the other. She lit the oven to roast it, and he climbed in and sat inside it, saying that one who does this act falls into this fire. She told him she would not have troubled him had she known.

stories.actor: Rav Kahana
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana while he was selling baskets, and he said he would go and prepare himself.
stories.turn: He went up to the roof and threw himself off, and Elijah came and caught him.
stories.outcome: Elijah complained he had come four hundred parasangs, and when Rav Kahana blamed his poverty, Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana was selling baskets when a noblewoman propositioned him. He told her he would go and adorn himself, then climbed onto the roof and threw himself down. Elijah caught him, complaining that he had been made to travel four hundred parasangs. Rav Kahana said poverty had put him in that position, and Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars.

stories.actor: The son of a widow, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
stories.event: A widow's son asked two sages whether father or mother takes precedence when both ask for water.
stories.turn: He then asked about a divorced mother, and Rabbi Yehoshua saw from his tearful eyes that he was a widow's son with no father.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua answered him sarcastically to pour water for them and call them like chickens.
stories.summary: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer, then Rabbi Yehoshua, whose request for water he should honor first, and both said the father's. He pressed on about a divorced mother. Rabbi Yehoshua, seeing from his tears that he was a widow's son, mocked the irrelevant question, saying he should pour water and squawk at them like chickens.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina, a gentile of Ashkelon
stories.event: The Sages wanted to buy merchandise from him for a huge profit.
stories.turn: The key was under his sleeping father's head.
stories.outcome: He would not wake his father, forgoing the profit (story continues past the window).
stories.summary: Asked how far honoring parents extends, Rav Ulla told of Dama ben Netina. The Sages sought to buy merchandise from him at a profit of six hundred thousand, but the key lay under his sleeping father's pillow, and he refused to disturb his father.

stories.actor: A man who came before Rabbi Ami
stories.event: He testified that someone had established priestly status by reading first in the synagogue.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami questioned whether he read first as a priest or as a great man; the man said a Levite read after him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood on his word.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Ami that another man was presumed a priest because he read first in synagogue. Rabbi Ami asked whether that might be due to his prominence, and the witness said a Levite read after him. Rabbi Ami accepted the testimony and elevated him to the priesthood.

stories.actor: A man who came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: He testified that someone was a Levite because he read second in the synagogue.
stories.turn: Asked whether that was due to prominence, he said a priest read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated the man to Levite status.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he read second in synagogue. When questioned, he explained that a priest had read first. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted it and elevated him to Levite status.

stories.actor: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: When a man testified to priestly status from Torah reading, Reish Lakish demanded evidence of receiving teruma, and Rabbi Elazar objected.
stories.turn: Later, before Rabbi Yochanan, the same objection came from Rabbi Yochanan himself, revealing that Rabbi Elazar had been quoting him.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yochanan by name.
stories.summary: Reish Lakish demanded proof that a reputed priest took teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar objected that priesthood does not cease where there is no threshing floor. On another occasion, Rabbi Yochanan made the same objection. Reish Lakish looked harshly at Rabbi Elazar and complained that he had heard this from Rabbi Yochanan without saying so.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and his wife
stories.event: Mar Ukva secretly left coins for a poor neighbor daily; one day the pauper came out to see who it was.
stories.turn: Fleeing, they hid in a hot furnace; only Mar Ukva's feet burned, and he was distraught.
stories.outcome: His wife explained her charity was greater because she gave food directly.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to slip four dinars through a poor neighbor's door every day. One day, delayed and accompanied by his wife, they were chased by the pauper who wanted to know his benefactor, and hid in a still-hot furnace. Mar Ukva's legs were singed while his wife's were not, which upset him; she explained that her charity of ready food was more immediate than his money.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and his son
stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his yearly Yom Kippur eve gift of four hundred dinars to a pauper via his son.
stories.turn: The son reported the pauper was spilling old wine for fragrance and did not need it.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva doubled the gift, reasoning he was so used to luxury.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva sent his son with the annual four hundred dinars for a poor neighbor. The son came back saying the man had no need, since they sprinkled old wine for him. Mar Ukva concluded the man was very pampered, doubled the money and sent it.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: On his deathbed he asked for his charity records and found seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He felt his provisions were too light for the long journey ahead.
stories.outcome: He gave away half his remaining wealth to charity.
stories.summary: As Mar Ukva lay dying he reviewed his charity accounts, which showed seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the way far, he rose and gave away half his estate. The Gemara then explains why this was permitted after death.

stories.actor: Rabbi Chanina and his wife
stories.event: Rabbi Chanina sent his weekly four dinars to a pauper via his wife.
stories.turn: She returned saying the man did not need it, because of what she overheard.
stories.outcome: Cut off at the window's edge.
stories.summary: Rabbi Chanina regularly sent four dinars to a poor man every Shabbat eve. Once his wife delivered it and came back saying he did not need it, as she had heard the household asking him what he dines on. The story continues beyond the window.

stories.actor: Rav Rechumi and his wife
stories.event: Rav Rechumi, who came home each Yom Kippur eve, stayed in the study hall engrossed in learning.
stories.turn: His waiting wife wept a tear of disappointment.
stories.outcome: At that moment the roof he sat on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rechumi studied with Rava in Mechoza and came home once a year on the eve of Yom Kippur. One year he was absorbed in study and did not come. His wife, expecting him, shed a tear, and the roof under him collapsed and he died.

stories.actor: Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yannai
stories.event: Yehuda came home every Friday at twilight preceded by a pillar of fire.
stories.turn: One week he stayed at study and Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared him dead.
stories.outcome: The ruler's mistaken word came true and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Chiyya and son-in-law of Rabbi Yannai, came home each Shabbat eve with a pillar of fire before him. Once he was absorbed in study and did not come. Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, said to overturn his bed, for he must be dead, and his word came true like a ruler's error: Yehuda died.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Chiyya's family
stories.event: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry a girl from Rabbi Chiyya's household.
stories.turn: When the marriage contract was being written, the girl died.
stories.outcome: They examined the lineages and found Rabbi descended from David and Rabbi Chiyya from David's brother.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi arranged a match between his son and a daughter of Rabbi Chiyya's family, but the girl died when the marriage contract was about to be written. Fearing a disqualification, they investigated the families. They found Rabbi descended from Shefatya ben Avital, David's wife, and Rabbi Chiyya from Shimi, David's brother.

stories.actor: Rava at his son's wedding
stories.event: Rava poured drinks for guests; some rabbis stood for him and two did not.
stories.turn: Rava took offense at those who did not stand.
stories.outcome: He angrily asked whether only they were Sages and the others not.
stories.summary: Serving guests at his son's wedding, Rava poured for Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, who stood up for him, and for Rav Mari and Rav Pinchas, who did not. Rava became angry and asked sarcastically whether those two were Sages while the others were not.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa at his son's wedding
stories.event: Rav Pappa poured a cup for Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda.
stories.turn: Rav Yitzchak did not stand for him.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa served drinks at the wedding of his son Abba Mar. When he poured for Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda, the latter did not rise, and Rav Pappa was offended.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: At his son's wedding Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, stood and served the sages drinks.
stories.turn: Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup and rebuked Rabbi Yehoshua for accepting it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua cited Abraham serving guests, and Rabbi Tzadok cited God Himself, justifying the service.
stories.summary: At Rabban Gamliel's son's wedding, the Nasi himself poured for the sages. Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup, but Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it, and Rabbi Eliezer protested. Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, greater still, served guests he took for Arabs, and Rabbi Tzadok added that God Himself sets a table for every creature.

stories.actor: A man who gave a conditional bill of divorce
stories.event: He said the divorce would take effect if he did not return within thirty days.
stories.turn: He arrived at the end of the thirty days but the ferry was on the other side, and he shouted that he had come.
stories.outcome: Shmuel ruled that this did not count as a return.
stories.summary: A man gave a bill of divorce on condition it take effect if he did not return within thirty days. He arrived on the last day but could not cross because the ferry was on the far bank, and called out, 'See that I have come.' Shmuel ruled that this was not a return.

stories.actor: Rav Chisda, a man who betrothed with a blue stone, and the man's mother
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a stone and Rav Chisda assessed whether it was worth a peruta.
stories.turn: The mother insisted it had been worth a peruta on the day, and the Sages noted witnesses elsewhere could confirm it.
stories.outcome: Rav Chisda held that she could not forbid the woman to others and that absent witnesses did not count.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a blue stone, and Rav Chisda appraised it to see if it was worth a peruta. The man's mother protested that it had been worth that on the day of betrothal, but Rav Chisda said she could not forbid the woman to a later suitor, citing a precedent. When the Sages objected that witnesses in Idit knew its value, he replied that they were not before him.

stories.actor: Yehudit, wife of Rabbi Chiyya
stories.event: Suffering painful childbirths, she told Rabbi Chiyya that her mother said she had been betrothed to someone else as a child.
stories.turn: Her claim would have made her forbidden to him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Chiyya said her mother had no power to forbid her to him.
stories.summary: Yehudit, Rabbi Chiyya's wife, had painful births and wanted out of the marriage. She told him her mother said her father had accepted a betrothal for her as a child. Rabbi Chiyya replied that her mother's word could not forbid her to him.

stories.actor: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi
stories.event: They sat at the entrance of King Izgur's house as the king's butler passed with food.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi noticed something about Mar Zutra.
stories.outcome: Cut off at the window's edge.
stories.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting at the gate of King Izgur when the royal butler went by carrying dishes. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra's reaction. The story continues beyond the window.

stories.actor: A beautiful woman
stories.event: Pursued by many suitors, she claimed she was already betrothed.
stories.turn: Later she betrothed herself, and the Sages asked why.
stories.outcome: She explained she had put off unworthy suitors and now accepted a worthy one; the Sages accepted her rationale.
stories.summary: A woman of great beauty was besieged by men wanting to marry her and told them she was betrothed. Later she betrothed herself to a man, and the Sages asked how. She said she had used that claim to fend off unscrupulous men and now accepted a decent one, and the Sages ruled such a rationale makes her credible.

stories.actor: Choma, Abaye's widow, Rava, and Rava's wife
stories.event: Choma asked Rava to award her sustenance and wine from Abaye's estate.
stories.turn: Gesturing to show the size of Abaye's cups, she bared her arm and her beauty lit up the court, and Rava went home aroused.
stories.outcome: Rava's wife learned who it was, chased Choma out of Mechoza with a chest lock, accusing her of killing three husbands.
stories.summary: After Abaye died, his widow Choma asked Rava for sustenance and then wine, and Rava doubted Abaye drank wine. She showed him how large Abaye's cups were, exposing her arm, and her beauty lit up the courtroom. Rava went home and sought his wife, who asked who had been in court; on hearing it was Choma, she beat her with a chest lock and drove her out of the city, saying she had already killed three husbands.

stories.actor: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya, and Rav Yosef
stories.event: She asked Rav Yosef to award her sustenance, wine and then silk garments.
stories.turn: He asked why she needed silk.
stories.outcome: She answered that it was for him, his friends and his friends' friends.
stories.summary: A widow came before Rav Yosef and received sustenance and wine from the estate. When she also asked for silk garments, he asked why. She retorted that it was for him and his colleagues, so she would not be shamed before them.

stories.actor: Rav Ashi and Rav Kahana
stories.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi to testify for him, but Rav Ashi did not remember and Rav Kahana prompted him.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi eventually remembered and testified, but Rav Kahana was hesitant to rely on it.
stories.outcome: Rav Ashi assured him he had remembered by his own effort, not by relying on him.
stories.summary: Rav Ashi knew testimony concerning Rav Kahana but said he did not remember it, even when Rav Kahana described what happened. Eventually Rav Ashi recalled it and testified. Seeing Rav Kahana uneasy, Rav Ashi told him he had not relied on his prompting but had remembered by his own effort.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride, and Rabban Gamliel the Elder
stories.event: A groom complained that he found no hymenal blood.
stories.turn: The bride said she came from the Dorketi family whose women have no blood, and Rabban Gamliel checked her relatives.
stories.outcome: Finding her claim true, he told the groom to keep his bride and congratulated him.
stories.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel the Elder complaining that his new wife showed no blood. She explained she was from the Dorketi family, whose women have neither menstrual nor hymenal blood. Rabban Gamliel investigated her relatives, confirmed it, and told the groom to take possession of his acquisition.

stories.actor: A starving couple and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
stories.event: A groom complained to Rabbi that he found no blood, while the bride insisted she was a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabbi saw their faces blackened by famine and had them bathed, fed and given drink.
stories.outcome: The groom then found blood, and Rabbi told him to keep his wife.
stories.summary: During years of drought, a groom told Rabbi he found no blood, and his bride said she was still a virgin. Seeing their famished faces, Rabbi had them bathed, fed and brought to a room. The groom then found blood, and Rabbi told him to take his acquisition, quoting a verse about skin shriveled on the bones.

stories.actor: A man who came before Rabbi Ami
stories.event: He testified that someone had priestly status because he read first in the synagogue.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami asked whether that might be due to prominence; he said a Levite read after him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Ami that another man was a presumed priest since he read first from the Torah. Asked if it was perhaps because of his stature, the witness said a Levite followed him. Rabbi Ami elevated him to the priesthood on that testimony.

stories.actor: A man who came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: He testified that someone was a Levite because he read second.
stories.turn: Questioned, he said a priest read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated him to Levite status.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he read second in synagogue. When asked if that reflected prominence, he said a priest had read first. The man was accorded Levite status on his word.

stories.actor: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Reish Lakish demanded evidence of teruma for a reputed priest and Rabbi Elazar objected.
stories.turn: Later Rabbi Yochanan made the same objection, revealing Rabbi Elazar had quoted him.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yochanan.
stories.summary: When a witness testified to priesthood from Torah reading, Reish Lakish asked if he had seen the man receive teruma, and Rabbi Elazar challenged that. Later, before Rabbi Yochanan, the same exchange happened with Rabbi Yochanan making the objection. Reish Lakish looked at Rabbi Elazar harshly and asked why he had not said it in Rabbi Yochanan's name.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva
stories.event: Rabbi Akiva mocked sinners, and Satan appeared to him as a woman atop a palm tree.
stories.turn: He began climbing the tree after her.
stories.outcome: Halfway up Satan left him, saying only heaven's protection had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva used to ridicule transgressors. Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and he started climbing. Halfway up, Satan released him, saying that were it not for heaven's warning to be careful with Rabbi Akiva, his life would have been worth nothing.

stories.actor: Peleimu
stories.event: Peleimu, who taunted Satan daily, was visited on Yom Kippur eve by Satan disguised as a repulsive pauper.
stories.turn: The pauper behaved disgustingly, was rebuked, and pretended to die, so people cried that Peleimu killed a man.
stories.outcome: Peleimu hid in shame; Satan revealed himself and told him to stop taunting and instead say 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan.'
stories.summary: Peleimu said every day, 'An arrow in Satan's eye.' On Yom Kippur eve Satan came as a pauper, demanded to be brought in and seated at the table, and acted revoltingly, then spat in a cup. When rebuked, he collapsed as if dead, and people cried that Peleimu had killed a man. Peleimu hid in the outhouse; Satan followed, revealed himself, and told him to pray for God to rebuke Satan instead.

stories.actor: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi and his wife
stories.event: His wife, puzzled by his prayer against the evil inclination though he had long abstained from her, disguised herself as the prostitute Charuta.
stories.turn: He propositioned her, and later, sitting in a hot oven in remorse, learned it had been his wife.
stories.outcome: He said he had intended to sin, and fasted the rest of his life until he died.
stories.summary: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi prayed daily to be saved from the evil inclination, which his wife found strange since he had withdrawn from her for years. She dressed up and passed him in his garden as Charuta the prostitute; he propositioned her and fetched her a pomegranate as payment. At home, he climbed into the burning oven in remorse; she proved it was she, but he said he had still intended to sin, and fasted all his days until he died.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and his wife
stories.event: Fleeing a pauper who wanted to identify his benefactors, they hid in a hot furnace.
stories.turn: Mar Ukva's legs burned while his wife's did not, and he was distraught.
stories.outcome: His wife explained her charity of food was more immediate than his.
stories.summary: When the pauper came out to see who was leaving money at his door, Mar Ukva and his wife ran and hid in a still-hot furnace. Mar Ukva's legs were scorched and his wife told him to rest them on hers, which upset him. She explained that her giving of ready food was greater than his giving of money.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and his son
stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his yearly gift of four hundred dinars to a pauper via his son.
stories.turn: The son reported the pauper lived in luxury, sprinkling old wine.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva doubled the gift.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva's son brought the annual Yom Kippur eve charity to a pauper and returned saying he did not need it, as they sprinkled old wine for him. Mar Ukva reasoned that he was so pampered, doubled the money and sent it.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: Dying, he reviewed his charity records showing seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He judged his provisions too light for the long way.
stories.outcome: He gave away half his wealth.
stories.summary: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity accounts and found seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the road long, he gave away half his money. The Gemara then explains why this was permitted.

stories.actor: Rabbi Chanina and his wife
stories.event: Rabbi Chanina sent his weekly charity to a pauper via his wife.
stories.turn: She overheard the household asking whether he dines on silver or gold tablecloths.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Chanina cited Rabbi Elazar's saying that we should be grateful to swindlers.
stories.summary: Rabbi Chanina used to send four dinars to a poor man every Shabbat eve. When his wife delivered it, she came back saying he did not need it, having heard them ask whether he dines on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Chanina quoted Rabbi Elazar that we should thank swindlers, without whom we would sin daily by neglecting the poor.

stories.actor: Rav Kahana
stories.event: Rav Kahana held beer belonging to the orphan Rav Mesharshiyya bar Chilkai.
stories.turn: Instead of selling it at once, he delayed until the Festival despite the risk of souring.
stories.outcome: He explained that at the Festival it would fetch ready cash.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana was holding beer that belonged to an orphan. He waited to sell it until the Festival, reasoning that even if it soured a little, it would bring in cash then.

stories.actor: Ravina and Rav Ashi
stories.event: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew and was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell.
stories.turn: He asked Rav Ashi whether he could take the orphan's wine along.
stories.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, as the orphan's wine was no better than his own.
stories.summary: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, Ravina the younger, and was taking his own wine to Sikhra for sale. He asked Rav Ashi if he could bring the orphan's wine too. Rav Ashi told him to go ahead, since it deserved no better treatment than his own.

stories.actor: Reish Lakish, his disseminator Yehuda bar Nachmani, and Rav Chiyya bar Abba
stories.event: Rav Chiyya bar Abba's child died and Reish Lakish came the next day with his disseminator to comfort him.
stories.turn: The disseminator's first words seemed to blame the father, and Reish Lakish directed him through a series of blessings.
stories.outcome: The disseminator delivered praises of God, words to the mourners, to the comforters, and a prayer for all Israel.
stories.summary: When the child of Rav Chiyya bar Abba, teacher of Reish Lakish's sons, died, Reish Lakish did not go the first day but the next day brought his disseminator to speak words of comfort. The disseminator opened with a verse attributing children's deaths to their fathers' sins, which the Gemara explains as meaning the father was worthy to be taken for his generation. Reish Lakish then had him speak in praise of God, to the mourners, to those who comfort them, and for all Israel, each ending in a blessing.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel
stories.event: Funerals had become so costly that relatives abandoned their dead and fled.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel instructed that he be buried in simple linen.
stories.outcome: Everyone followed his example, and plain burial became the custom.
stories.summary: Funeral costs once burdened families more than the death itself, until people would abandon the body and flee. Rabban Gamliel set an example of humility by ordering that he be buried in plain linen garments. All the people followed him, and Rav Pappa notes that today people are buried even in cheap rough cloth.

stories.actor: A man who sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: He sold his property intending to go to Eretz Yisrael and went.
