stories.turn: He could not settle there and returned, seeking to cancel the sale.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled (in one version) that he could cancel it, since he went to settle; in another version, that he could not.
stories.summary: A man sold his property, stating he intended to move to Eretz Yisrael. He went but was unable to settle and came back wanting to void the sale. Rava ruled that he could, since the intention was to settle; others report Rava ruled the sale stands since he did go.

stories.actor: A man who sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: He sold his property intending to go to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: In the end he did not go.
stories.outcome: Rav Ashi ruled that the sale stands, since he could have gone had he wanted.
stories.summary: Another man sold his property in order to move to Eretz Yisrael but never went. Rav Ashi ruled that he could have gone if he wished, so the sale was not voided.

stories.actor: Ravin the Pious
stories.event: Ravin went to betroth a woman for his son.
stories.turn: Her family would not give her to the son, so he betrothed her to himself.
stories.outcome: He did not first inform his son, fearing someone else would betroth her meanwhile.
stories.summary: Ravin the Pious went as agent to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her to himself. The Gemara explains that her family would not give her to the son, and he acted at once lest someone else betroth her while he went to tell his son.

stories.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Chana
stories.event: Rabba bar bar Chana gave Rav money to buy land for him.
stories.turn: Rav bought the land for himself.
stories.outcome: It was explained that the violent locals would sell only to Rav, and he feared losing it if he delayed.
stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Chana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land for him, but Rav bought it for himself. The land was in a valley of violent men who respected Rav and not Rabba bar bar Chana, and Rav acted quickly lest another buyer take it.

stories.actor: Rav Giddel, Rabbi Abba, and Rav Yitzchak Nappacha
stories.event: Rabbi Abba bought land Rav Giddel was negotiating for, and Rav Giddel complained up the chain to Rav Yitzchak Nappacha.
stories.turn: At the Festival, Rav Yitzchak asked Rabbi Abba about a pauper whose loaf is snatched, and Rabbi Abba conceded such a person is wicked, saying he had not known.
stories.outcome: Refusing to sell his first land, Rabbi Abba offered it to Rav Giddel as a gift.
stories.summary: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a plot when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who complained to Rav Yitzchak Nappacha, who waited until Rabbi Abba came for the Festival and posed the case of a poor man whose bread is snatched. Rabbi Abba said the snatcher is wicked, explained he had not known, and, unwilling to sell his first land as a bad omen, offered it to Rav Giddel as a gift.

stories.actor: A man in Mata Mechasya and his brother
stories.event: The man's widowed sister-in-law fell to him for levirate marriage, and his brother wanted to disqualify her with a bill of divorce.
stories.turn: The man offered to split the inheritance, but the brother feared being cheated like the swindler of Pumbedita.
stories.outcome: The man offered to divide the property right away.
stories.summary: A man in Mata Mechasya was due to perform levirate marriage, and his brother sought to block it by giving her a bill of divorce. The man asked if it was about the estate and offered to share it. The brother said he feared being tricked as the Pumbedita swindler had done, so the man offered to divide it with him immediately.

stories.actor: an unmarried man and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A never-married man told Rav Nahman he had found an unobstructed orifice on his wedding night.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman inferred he could only know this from experience with prostitutes.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ordered him flogged with palm branches.
stories.summary: A man who had never been married complained to Rav Nahman that his bride was not a virgin. Rav Nahman reasoned that such a man could only know this if he had been with prostitutes, and ordered him flogged with palm branches.

stories.actor: a man and Rabban Gamliel
stories.event: A man claimed before Rabban Gamliel that he had found his bride not a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested he had diverted his approach, illustrating with a parable of a door found open or locked.
stories.outcome: The man's claim was cast into doubt by Rabban Gamliel's explanation.
stories.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel claiming he found an unobstructed orifice. Rabban Gamliel suggested he had entered at an angle, comparing it to someone in the dark who finds a door open only because he moved the bolt.

stories.actor: a groom, his bride, and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom complained he found no blood after consummating the marriage, while the bride insisted she was a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel had the cloth soaked and laundered, revealing drops of blood.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to go and take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: A groom told Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi that he found no blood, and the bride said she had been a virgin. The judge had the cloth brought, soaked and washed, and found drops of blood on it. He told the groom his bride was a virgin and to keep his acquisition.

stories.actor: a purchaser and a creditor
stories.event: The purchaser took one hundred dinars to the creditor and offered him a choice.
stories.turn: He told the creditor to accept the repossessed tract as full payment or take the money and give up both tracts.
stories.outcome: Not stated in the window.
stories.summary: A purchaser went to a creditor with one hundred dinars and said: if the tract you took is worth a hundred to you, keep it; otherwise take the money and withdraw from both tracts.

stories.actor: orphans, their father's creditor, and Abaye
stories.event: A creditor repossessed the dead man's small field, the orphans paid fifty dinars to redeem it, and the creditor seized it again.
stories.turn: The orphans complained to Abaye.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled their payment was a mitzva toward their father's debt and the creditor's second seizure was lawful.
stories.summary: A man died owing one hundred dinars and left land worth fifty. The creditor seized it, the orphans paid him fifty to redeem it, and he seized it again. Abaye told them their payment was a mitzva toward their father's debt, so the creditor's repossession stood.

stories.actor: a man who sold his mother's marriage contract
stories.event: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract, saying he would not reimburse the buyer if his mother objected.
stories.turn: His mother died without objecting, and he himself contested the sale.
stories.outcome: Rava held that he had guaranteed the sale against his own objections.
stories.summary: A man sold his future rights to his mother's marriage contract, disclaiming responsibility if she objected. After she died without objecting, he tried to contest the sale himself. Rami bar Hama thought he stood in his mother's place, but Rava said he had certainly guaranteed it against his own challenge.

stories.actor: orphans, their father's creditor, and Abaye
stories.event: A creditor repossessed the dead man's small field, the orphans paid fifty dinars to redeem it, and the creditor seized it again.
stories.turn: The orphans complained to Abaye.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled their payment was a mitzva toward their father's debt and the second seizure was lawful.
stories.summary: A man died owing one hundred dinars and left land worth fifty. The creditor seized it, the orphans paid him fifty, and he seized it again. Abaye told them they had performed a mitzva by paying part of their father's debt, so the creditor's seizure was lawful.

stories.actor: a man who sold his mother's marriage contract
stories.event: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract, disclaiming liability if she objected.
stories.turn: His mother died without objecting, and he himself contested the sale.
stories.outcome: Rava held that he had guaranteed the sale against his own objections.
stories.summary: A man sold his future rights to his mother's marriage contract, saying he would not reimburse the buyer if she objected. She died without objecting, and he then challenged the sale. Rava rejected him, since he had surely guaranteed it against his own challenge.

stories.actor: a Madonite in Jerusalem
stories.event: A Madonite with much movable property wished to give it as a gift and was told it could only be transferred by means of land.
stories.turn: He bought a beit sela of land near Jerusalem and gave a northern portion with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages fulfilled his instructions.
stories.summary: A Madonite in Jerusalem wanted to give away his movable property but was told he needed land to transfer it. He bought a small plot near Jerusalem and gave part of it to someone along with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. He died, and the Sages carried out his gift.

stories.actor: a man in Jerusalem
stories.event: A man (sick or healthy) wished to give away much movable property and was told he needed land to do it.
stories.turn: He acquired a beit rova of land and gave a square handbreadth with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages fulfilled his statement.
stories.summary: A man in Jerusalem with much movable property wanted to give it away and was told it could only be done through land. He bought a small plot and gave a handbreadth of it with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. After he died the Sages honored his gift.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: Rabbi Elazar, who never testified, testified once about seeing teruma given.
stories.turn: Because he saw it where teruma did not imply priesthood and testified where it did, the court nearly elevated a slave to priesthood.
stories.outcome: They sought to elevate the slave on his testimony but did not.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei said he testified only once in his life, and on his word a court nearly made a slave a priest. He had seen a priest's slave receive teruma in Rabbi Yosei's region and testified in Rabbi Yehuda's region, where receiving teruma proved priestly lineage. The Gemara says the slave was not actually elevated.

stories.actor: Ulla and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Ulla, who regularly went up to Eretz Yisrael, died outside the land.
stories.turn: Rabbi Elazar lamented him, and when told his coffin was coming, said burial after death is not like being absorbed by the land while alive.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Elazar maintained his lament despite the coffin's arrival.
stories.summary: Ulla used to travel to Eretz Yisrael but died abroad. When Rabbi Elazar heard, he applied to him the verse about dying in an unclean land. Told that the coffin was being brought for burial, he replied that being received by the land in death is not like being received in life.

stories.actor: a man from Eretz Yisrael and Rabbi Hanina
stories.event: A man whose brother died abroad asked Rabbi Hanina if he could go down to Babylonia to marry the widow.
stories.turn: Rabbi Hanina called the brother's wife a Samaritan and blessed God for killing him.
stories.outcome: He told the man not to follow his brother out of the land.
stories.summary: A man's brother died leaving a widow in far-off Bei Hoza'a, and he asked Rabbi Hanina if he could go down to perform levirate marriage. Rabbi Hanina answered that his brother had married a 'Samaritan' and God had killed him for leaving the land, so why should he follow?

stories.actor: a man who left Pumbedita
stories.event: A man left Pumbedita to live in Bei Kuvei.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef excommunicated him.
stories.outcome: He was excommunicated.
stories.summary: A man moved from Pumbedita to Bei Kuvei, outside Babylonia proper, and Rav Yosef excommunicated him for it.

stories.actor: a Torah scholar who left Pumbedita
stories.event: A scholar left Pumbedita for Astonia.
stories.turn: He died there.
stories.outcome: Abaye said that had he wished, he would still be alive.
stories.summary: A scholar left Pumbedita to live in Astonia and died. Abaye remarked that he would have lived had he chosen to stay in Babylonia.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya bar Adda and Reish Lakish
stories.event: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, a schoolteacher, missed three days of teaching.
stories.turn: He explained he was harvesting a vine whose yield dropped each day, and Reish Lakish said the yield would have been greater had he not neglected the children.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish rebuked him.
stories.summary: Reish Lakish's schoolteacher disappeared for three days. He explained he was harvesting an amazingly fruitful vine his father left him, which yielded less wine each day. Reish Lakish told him that if he had not abandoned the children's lessons, it would have produced even more.

stories.actor: Rami bar Yehezkel
stories.event: Rami bar Yehezkel came to Benei Berak and saw goats under a fig tree with honey and milk dripping and mixing.
stories.turn: He recognized the sight as the meaning of the verse.
stories.outcome: He declared this is 'a land flowing with milk and honey.'
stories.summary: Visiting Benei Berak, Rami bar Yehezkel saw goats grazing under fig trees, with fig honey and goat milk dripping and mixing together. He said: this is what 'flowing with milk and honey' means.

stories.actor: Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai
stories.event: Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai set out early one morning from Lud toward Ono.
stories.turn: He found himself walking ankle-deep in fig honey.
stories.outcome: He reported the land's abundance.
stories.summary: Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai recalled rising early to walk the three mil from Lud to Ono and wading ankle-deep in honey oozing from fig trees.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Three Sages visiting a place were served a peach as big as a five-se'a pot and divided it in thirds.
stories.turn: A year later Rabbi Elazar was served a peach there small enough to hold in one hand.
stories.outcome: He quoted the verse about a fruitful land turned to salt because of its inhabitants' wickedness.
stories.summary: Three Sages came to a town and were given an enormous peach; they ate a third, left a third ownerless, and fed a third to their animals. The next year Rabbi Elazar visited and the peach fit in his hand. He cited the verse that a fruitful land becomes a salt waste because of the wickedness of its people.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi came to Gavla and saw grape clusters as large as calves.
stories.turn: He mistook them for calves among the vines and was told they were clusters.
stories.outcome: He cried out to the land to withhold its fruit from the gentiles ruling over Israel.
stories.summary: In Gavla, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw what looked like calves standing among the vines and asked about them. Told they were grape clusters, he called on the land to gather in its fruit rather than produce it for the gentiles who ruled over them.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives
stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized an orphans' cow for a debt.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yohanan approved but Reish Lakish ordered them to return it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he could do nothing since an equal disagreed with him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives took an orphans' cow to cover a debt. Rabbi Yohanan told them they had done well, but Reish Lakish told them to give it back. When they returned to Rabbi Yohanan, he said he could not help them, since a scholar of equal stature disagreed.

stories.actor: a herdsman, a creditor, and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, claiming it was before the debtor's death.
stories.turn: The herdsman claimed it was after, but had no witnesses to the seizure.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the creditor by a 'since he could claim' argument.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from a herdsman tending orphans' cattle, saying he seized it while their father was alive; the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman asked whether there were witnesses to the seizure, and there were none. He ruled the creditor could keep it, since he could have claimed he bought it.

stories.actor: the house of the Nasi and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: The Nasi's household seized an orphans' maidservant for a debt.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abbahu approved, but Rabbi Abba accused the judges of flattering the Nasi and cited Reish Lakish's reversal of such a ruling.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba rebuked the court.
stories.summary: Members of the Nasi's house seized a maidservant belonging to orphans. Rabbi Abbahu, judging with colleagues, said they had done well. Rabbi Abba objected that they were currying favor with the powerful, since Reish Lakish had already overturned such a ruling.

stories.actor: Yeimar bar Hashu, Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: Yeimar bar Hashu had his agent seize a dead debtor's boat.
stories.turn: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna told him the seizure was invalid because it harmed other creditors, then seized the boat themselves.
stories.outcome: When Rav Pinehas bar Ami challenged them, they said they had seized it in the river's current, a public domain.
stories.summary: A debtor of Yeimar bar Hashu died leaving a boat, and Yeimar's agent seized it. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, also creditors, ruled the seizure invalid and grabbed the boat themselves, one with an oar and one with a rope, each claiming all of it. When Rav Pinehas bar Ami objected that seizure needs a public domain, they answered they had taken it in the middle of the river.

stories.actor: an unmarried man and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A never-married man told Rav Nahman he found an unobstructed orifice.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman inferred he must have consorted with prostitutes.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ordered him flogged with palm branches.
stories.summary: A man who had never been married claimed before Rav Nahman that his bride was not a virgin. Rav Nahman concluded he could only know this from prostitutes and ordered him flogged.

stories.actor: a man and Rabban Gamliel
stories.event: A man claimed before Rabban Gamliel that he found his bride not a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested he had diverted his approach, with a parable about a door.
stories.outcome: The claim was cast into doubt.
stories.summary: A man told Rabban Gamliel he found an unobstructed orifice. Rabban Gamliel suggested he had approached at an angle, like a man in the dark who finds a door open only because he moved its bolt.

stories.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil and Shmuel
stories.event: Rav Yosef of Dabil issued a practical ruling following Rav against Shmuel.
stories.turn: Shmuel took offense.
stories.outcome: Shmuel sarcastically asked whether wisdom had been measured out to him in a large measure.
stories.summary: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil decided a real case according to Rav's view. Shmuel was offended and mocked him, asking whether wisdom was given to everyone in a small measure but to this man in a large one.

stories.actor: the sons of bar Tzartzur, Rav Amram and Rav Nahman
stories.event: The estate of bar Tzartzur grew in value, and his sons by two wives came before Rav Amram.
stories.turn: Rav Amram told one set of sons to appease the others; they refused, and he threatened them with excommunication and sent them to Rav Nahman.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled the heirs' rights were fixed at the father's death.
stories.summary: Bar Tzartzur's estate was too small to pay his wives' marriage contracts at his death but later grew. Rav Amram urged the sons of the larger contract to appease their half-brothers, and when they ignored him he threatened to excommunicate them and sent them to Rav Nahman. Rav Nahman ruled that, as when an estate shrinks, the heirs' rights are set at the time of death.

stories.actor: a debtor, purchaser and creditor
stories.event: A man owing a thousand dinars sold two mansions for five hundred each, and the creditor repossessed one and then sought the other.
stories.turn: The purchaser brought a thousand dinars and offered the creditor a choice.
stories.outcome: Cut off at the window's edge.
stories.summary: A man owed a thousand dinars and sold his two mansions for five hundred each. His creditor took one from the buyer and then went after the second. The buyer came with a thousand dinars and said: accept the first mansion as full payment, or take this money and give up both.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his sons
stories.event: At the time of his passing, Rabbi summoned his sons.
stories.turn: He gave them his last instructions about their stepmother's honor, his lamp, table and bed, and his attendants.
stories.outcome: His instructions were given.
stories.summary: As he was dying, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called for his sons. He told them to honor their mother, to keep his lamp lit, table set and bed made in their places, and that Yosef Heifani and Shimon Efrati, who served him in life, would serve him in death.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi after death
stories.event: After his death Rabbi would return home every Shabbat eve.
stories.turn: One Shabbat eve a neighbor knocked and his maidservant told her to be quiet because Rabbi was sitting there.
stories.outcome: Once his presence was revealed, he never came again.
stories.summary: Rabbi asked that his lamp, table and bed be kept in place because he would come home each Shabbat eve after his death. One week a neighbor came knocking, and the maid hushed her, saying Rabbi was sitting there. Once word got out, he stopped coming, so as not to cast aspersions on earlier righteous men.

stories.actor: Yosef Heifani and Shimon Efrati
stories.event: Rabbi said his two attendants would serve him in his death, which people took to mean his burial.
stories.turn: The two died before him.
stories.outcome: People understood he meant they would serve him in the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: Rabbi said his attendants Yosef Heifani and Shimon Efrati would serve him in death, and people assumed he meant they would bury him. When their biers went out before his, they understood he meant the next world.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages
stories.event: Rabbi summoned the Sages and told them not to eulogize him in the towns and appointed his successors.
stories.turn: People thought he wanted to spare them trouble, but when eulogies were held in the cities and everyone came, they understood he meant honor.
stories.outcome: He was eulogized in the cities with great crowds.
stories.summary: Dying, Rabbi called in the Sages, told them not to eulogize him in small towns and to reopen the yeshiva after thirty days, and named Gamliel as Nasi and Hanina bar Hama as head. People assumed the town instruction was to save trouble, but when the eulogies in the cities drew everyone, they realized it was for his honor.

stories.actor: a launderer
stories.event: A Divine Voice declared everyone at Rabbi's funeral destined for the World-to-Come, but a launderer who came to Rabbi daily had missed it.
stories.turn: On hearing this, he climbed to the roof, threw himself down and died.
stories.outcome: A Divine Voice declared that he too was destined for the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: On the day of Rabbi's funeral a heavenly voice promised the World-to-Come to all who attended. A launderer who visited Rabbi every day had not come that day; when he heard, he jumped from a roof and died. A heavenly voice then announced that he too was destined for the World-to-Come.

stories.actor: Abaye and his tenant farmer
stories.event: Abaye permitted his tenant to betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef told Abaye that Rav and Shmuel require twenty-four months.
stories.outcome: Abaye ran three parasangs after the tenant but could not catch him.
stories.summary: Abaye's tenant asked whether he could betroth a nursing widow after fifteen months, and Abaye said yes, citing several authorities. When he told Rav Yosef, Rav Yosef cited Rav and Shmuel requiring twenty-four months. Abaye ran three parasangs, some say through sand, to stop the tenant, but never caught up.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, and an old woman
stories.event: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna planned to rule leniently, following a baraita, that a nursing mother who gave her child to a wet nurse may remarry immediately.
stories.turn: An old woman told them that Rav Nahman had forbidden it in her own case.
stories.outcome: Her testimony challenged their intended ruling.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua were about to permit a nursing mother to remarry at once, following a baraita. An old woman told them that this had happened to her, and Rav Nahman had forbidden it.

stories.actor: Rami bar Hama, Mar Ukva, Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman
stories.event: Rav Sheshet awarded property to Rami bar Hama and Rav Nahman awarded it to his brother Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: Rav Sheshet confronted Rav Nahman, whose reasons proved stronger.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman asserted that he was a judge and Rav Sheshet was not, and that his reasoning had been flawed from the start.
stories.summary: Rami bar Hama came to Rav Sheshet and was awarded the property; his brother Mar Ukva went to Rav Nahman and was awarded it too. Rav Sheshet asked Rav Nahman why, saying Rami's deed came first; Rav Nahman replied that hours are not written in Babylonian deeds and he had used judicial discretion. When Rav Sheshet claimed discretion too, Rav Nahman said he was an official judge and Rav Sheshet was not, and Rav Sheshet had not reasoned that way originally.

stories.actor: two deed holders and Rav Yosef
stories.event: Two deeds for the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just 'Nisan'.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef awarded the field to the dated deed; the loser asked for authorization to repossess from later buyers.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef refused, since buyers could claim his deed was from the first of Nisan.
stories.summary: Two people with deeds to the same field came to Rav Yosef. He gave it to the one dated the fifth of Nisan, telling the other his undated deed might be from the twenty-ninth. When the loser asked for a document to collect from property sold after Iyyar, Rav Yosef said buyers could reply that his deed was from the first of Nisan, making the field his after all.

stories.actor: a man named Yohanan and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
stories.event: A man speaking offhandedly recalled being carried from school as a child and immersed to eat teruma that evening.
stories.turn: He added that friends shunned him and called him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'.
stories.outcome: Rabbi elevated him to the priesthood on his word.
stories.summary: A man mentioned in passing that as a child on his father's shoulders he was taken out of school and immersed so he could eat teruma that evening, and that his friends avoided him and called him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'. On the basis of this offhand remark, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recognized him as a priest.

stories.actor: Shmuel
stories.event: As Shmuel stepped off a ferry, a man gave him a hand.
stories.turn: The man revealed he had a case to bring before Shmuel.
stories.outcome: Shmuel disqualified himself from the case.
stories.summary: A man helped Shmuel off a ferry. When Shmuel asked his business, the man said he had a case for him, and Shmuel declared himself disqualified from judging it.

stories.actor: Ameimar
stories.event: While Ameimar was judging, a feather landed on his head and a man removed it.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A feather drifted onto Ameimar's head as he sat in judgment, and a man brushed it off. Learning the man had a case, Ameimar said he could not judge it.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: A man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered some spittle in front of Mar Ukva. When he said he had a case, Mar Ukva disqualified himself from judging it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei and his sharecropper
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the usual Friday fruit basket on Thursday instead.
stories.turn: He explained he had a case and brought it on his way; Rabbi Yishmael refused it and appointed other judges, yet found himself mentally arguing the man's side.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers, realizing how even a refused gift had biased him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper, who brought fruit every Friday, came on Thursday and admitted he had a court case. Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit, disqualified himself, and seated two other scholars. Pacing nearby, he caught himself thinking up arguments for the sharecropper and exclaimed: if I, who took nothing that was not mine, am this biased, how much more those who take bribes.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha
stories.event: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael, a priest, the first shearing from a distant place.
stories.turn: Asked why he passed other priests, he admitted he had a case; Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and appointed other judges, yet found himself mentally arguing for the man.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: A man brought the first shearing to Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha from far away. Asked why he had not given it to a nearer priest, he said he had a case. Rabbi Yishmael refused it and had two scholars judge, but caught himself thinking up the man's arguments and exclaimed how much worse it must be for those who actually take bribes.

stories.actor: Rav Anan
stories.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Rav Anan refused the fish and disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish. When he said he had a case, Rav Anan refused the gift and disqualified himself.

stories.actor: Shmuel
stories.event: As Shmuel stepped off a ferry, a man gave him a hand.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Shmuel disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man helped Shmuel off a ferry. Learning that he had a case, Shmuel declared himself disqualified from judging it.

stories.actor: Ameimar
stories.event: While Ameimar was judging, a man removed a feather from his head.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man brushed a feather off Ameimar's head while he was judging. When the man said he had a case, Ameimar disqualified himself.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: A man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered spittle in front of Mar Ukva, then said he had a case. Mar Ukva disqualified himself.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei and his sharecropper
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the Friday fruit basket on Thursday.
stories.turn: He admitted he had a case; Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and appointed other judges, but found himself arguing the man's side in his mind.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper brought his weekly fruit a day early because he had a court case. Rabbi Yishmael refused it and had two scholars judge, but caught himself mentally pleading the sharecropper's case. He exclaimed that if he was so affected, how much more those who take bribes.

stories.actor: Rav Avya and his wife, sister of Rami bar Hama
stories.event: The marriage contract of Rav Avya's wife was lost.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef first said only Rabbi Meir requires a contract, but Abaye pointed out the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's decrees.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef told Rav Avya to write her a new marriage contract.
stories.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister, married to Rav Avya, lost her marriage contract, and the couple came to Rav Yosef. He said the strict view that they may not live together without it is only Rabbi Meir's, but Abaye objected that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's decrees. Rav Yosef then told Rav Avya to go write her a new one.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hanina bar Hama
stories.event: In Rabbi's days, people sought to declare Babylonian lineage inferior to that of Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: Rabbi, of Babylonian descent, protested and sent Rabbi Hanina bar Hama to address them.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hanina cited a tradition that Babylonian lineage is the purest.
stories.summary: In Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's time some wanted to rank Babylonian lineage below Eretz Yisrael's. Rabbi, whose family came from Babylonia, asked if they meant to put thorns in his eyes and sent Rabbi Hanina bar Hama to them. Rabbi Hanina told them his received tradition was that Eretz Yisrael's lineage is muddled compared to Babylonia's.

stories.actor: Rabbi Pinehas
stories.event: In Rabbi Pinehas's days, people sought to declare Babylonian lineage inferior.
stories.turn: He arranged for servants to carry him off, distracted the study hall with a startling ruling, then declared Eretz Yisrael's lineage inferior to Babylonia's and fled.
stories.outcome: His pursuers failed to catch him, investigated lineages until it became dangerous, and stopped.
stories.summary: When some in Rabbi Pinehas's day wanted to declare Babylonian lineage inferior, he told his servants to carry him away on a stretcher after he made two statements. In the study hall he first said bird slaughter is not required by Torah law, and while they puzzled over it he declared Eretz Yisrael's lineage muddled compared to Babylonia's. They chased him in vain, then began checking family lineages until it grew dangerous and they gave up.

stories.actor: Ze'eiri and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: Ze'eiri kept avoiding Rabbi Yohanan's offer to marry his daughter.
stories.turn: When Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan across a puddle, Rabbi Yohanan asked why his Torah was worthy but not his daughters.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan argued that Babylonian lineage is no purer; the Gemara notes he missed Rabbi Elazar's teaching.
stories.summary: The Babylonian scholar Ze'eiri avoided Rabbi Yohanan, who kept urging him to marry his daughter. One day Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan across a pool of water, and Rabbi Yohanan asked why his Torah was fit for honor but his daughters were not fit to marry, arguing that flawed lineages remained in Babylonia too.

stories.actor: Ulla and Rav Yehuda
stories.event: Ulla visited Rav Yehuda and saw his grown son unmarried.
stories.turn: Rav Yehuda said he did not know where to find a wife of sound lineage, and Ulla answered that no one knows his own descent.
stories.outcome: Ulla pressed the point with verses suggesting all might be of tainted descent; the exchange runs to the window's edge.
stories.summary: Ulla came to Rav Yehuda's house in Pumbedita and saw that his son Rav Yitzhak was grown but unmarried. Rav Yehuda said he did not know where to find a suitable wife. Ulla replied that none of us knows our own ancestry, since we might descend from women ravished in Zion or from the decadent people Amos describes.

stories.actor: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host and Rav Beivai
stories.event: The host, son of a convert, and Rav Beivai quarreled over who would hold the city's public office and came before Rav Yosef.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef ruled that a convert may hold no office, but Rav Adda bar Ahava asked whether this applies when the mother is Jewish.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled such a man is fit, so Rav Beivai oversaw heavenly matters and the host oversaw the city's affairs; Abaye drew the moral to host a scholar like Rav Adda.
stories.summary: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host, the son of a convert, competed with Rav Beivai for a city post, and they brought the dispute to Rav Yosef. Rav Yosef first said converts cannot be appointed, but Rav Adda asked about one whose mother was born Jewish. Rav Yosef said such a man counts as 'from among your brothers,' and divided the duties: Rav Beivai over religious matters, the host over civic ones. Abaye remarked that one should host a scholar like Rav Adda who pleads in his host's favor.

stories.actor: Hama son of Rabba bar Abbahu
stories.event: Hama's case came before Rabbi Abbahu, who asked whether he had witnesses that he had paid.
stories.turn: Hama had no witnesses.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu ruled the other side could claim the debts were separate, so Hama could demand neither the money nor the document.
stories.summary: A case involving Hama came before Rabbi Abbahu. Asked whether he had witnesses to his payment, Hama said no. Rabbi Abbahu ruled that since the others could have denied the payment entirely, they could also claim it was for other debts, and Hama lost.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
stories.event: Heirs claimed a bag of documents deposited with her, and she said she had seized it from the deceased while he was alive.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that the deceased had demanded it in his lifetime and she refused; she had none.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled it was a seizure after death, which is ineffective.
stories.summary: A woman held a bag of documents that had been deposited with her, and the heirs demanded it. She claimed she had seized it during the owner's lifetime against a debt. Rav Nahman asked for witnesses, she had none, and he ruled her seizure counted as after death and was void.

stories.actor: Rava and his wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda
stories.event: A woman was obligated to take an oath in Rava's court.
stories.turn: Rav Hisda's daughter told Rava she knew the woman was suspect regarding oaths.
stories.outcome: Rava reversed the oath onto the opposing party.
stories.summary: A woman was required to swear in Rava's court. Rava's wife, Rav Hisda's daughter, told him the woman was known to swear falsely. Rava shifted the oath to the other litigant.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa, Rav Adda bar Mattana and Rava
stories.event: Rav Pappa told Rava that a document brought to court had already been paid.
stories.turn: Rava refused to act on a single witness, and Rav Adda bar Mattana challenged him since he had relied on Rav Hisda's daughter.
stories.outcome: Rava explained he knew with certainty that his wife was truthful but did not have that certainty about Rav Pappa.
stories.summary: While Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana sat before Rava, a document came to court and Rav Pappa testified it was paid. Rava said one witness is nothing. Rav Adda asked why Rav Pappa was worth less than Rav Hisda's daughter, whom Rava had trusted; Rava answered that he was certain of her honesty but not of Rav Pappa's.

stories.actor: Shimon (or Nehemya) HaAmasoni
stories.event: He interpreted every occurrence of 'et' in the Torah until he reached 'You shall fear (et) the Lord your God.'
stories.turn: He withdrew from the whole method, and his students asked what would become of all his earlier interpretations.
stories.outcome: He said he was rewarded for the withdrawal as for the exposition; later Rabbi Akiva explained the verse to include Torah scholars.
stories.summary: Shimon HaAmasoni expounded every 'et' in the Torah, but stopped when he reached the verse about fearing God, since nothing could share that fear. His students asked about all his previous expositions, and he replied that he was rewarded for abandoning them just as for making them. The verse remained unexplained until Rabbi Akiva taught that it includes fear of Torah scholars.

stories.actor: A witness before Rabbi Ami
stories.event: A man testified to Rabbi Ami that another had presumptive status as a priest because he read first in the synagogue.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami asked whether he read first as a priest or as a great man; the witness said a Levite read after him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood on his word.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Ami that someone was presumed a priest because he was called first to the Torah. Rabbi Ami questioned whether that was due to his stature, and the man answered that a Levite read next. Rabbi Ami then accepted him as a priest.

stories.actor: A witness before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: A man testified that another was a Levite because he read second in the synagogue.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked whether it was due to his stature; the witness said a priest read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated him to Levite status.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was presumed a Levite because he read second. When asked whether that reflected his prominence, he said a priest had read first. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted the man as a Levite.

stories.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: Reish Lakish demanded that a witness to priestly status show the man had received teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar objected.
stories.turn: When the same case came before Rabbi Yohanan, he gave exactly Rabbi Elazar's objection, revealing Elazar had been quoting him.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name.
stories.summary: A man testified before Reish Lakish that someone was a priest because he read first, and Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him take teruma at the threshing floor. Rabbi Elazar retorted that priesthood does not lapse where there is no threshing floor. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same thing happened and Rabbi Yohanan said the very same words. Reish Lakish looked harshly at Rabbi Elazar and complained that he had heard it from Rabbi Yohanan and not said so.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan and his relatives
stories.event: His relatives, who had to pay for their father's widow's daily medical treatment, asked Rabbi Yohanan what to do.
stories.turn: He advised them to fix a lump sum with the doctor so the cost would be deducted from her marriage contract.
stories.outcome: He later regretted it, saying he had acted like a legal advisor, since an important person should not favor his relatives this way.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives were supporting their father's widow, who needed treatment every day. He told them to agree on a fixed fee with the doctor, which would shift the cost onto her marriage contract. Afterwards he regretted it, saying he had made himself like a lawyer; a man of his standing should not tilt the law toward his family.

stories.actor: Ravina
stories.event: Ravina arranged his son's match with the house of Rav Haviva and began the wedding blessing from the betrothal, certain they would not back out.
stories.turn: The other family retracted.
stories.outcome: The wedding never happened.
stories.summary: Ravina betrothed his son to a woman of Rav Haviva's family and started reciting the wedding blessing from the betrothal, sure the marriage would go through. Nevertheless the family withdrew and the match was cancelled.

stories.actor: Rav Amram the Pious
stories.event: Redeemed captive women were lodged in his attic with the ladder removed, and seized by desire for one he lifted a ladder ten men could not carry and began to climb.
stories.turn: Halfway up he stopped himself and shouted 'Fire in the house of Amram!'
stories.outcome: The Sages came and said he shamed them; he replied that was better than shame in the World-to-Come, then adjured his evil inclination to leave him, and it left like a pillar of fire.
stories.summary: Captive women brought to Neharde'a were housed in Rav Amram's upper room and the ladder was taken away. When he glimpsed one of them, he single-handedly lifted a huge ladder and started up, but halfway he braced himself and cried 'Fire!' The Sages who rushed in complained he embarrassed them; he said shame in this world was better than in the next. He then forced his evil inclination out, saw it leave as a pillar of fire, and told it that he, mere flesh, had beaten it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Meir
stories.event: Rabbi Meir mocked sinners, and Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river, so he started crossing by a rope bridge.
stories.turn: Halfway across, Satan let him go.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning to protect Rabbi Meir and his Torah had kept him from ruining him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at transgressors. Satan appeared as a woman on the far bank of a river, and Rabbi Meir began crossing by a rope bridge to reach her. Halfway across Satan released him, saying that were it not for heaven's proclamation to protect Rabbi Meir, he would have made his life worthless.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva
stories.event: Rabbi Akiva mocked sinners, and Satan appeared to him as a woman atop a palm tree, so he began to climb.
stories.turn: Halfway up, Satan let him go.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning to protect Rabbi Akiva had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also scoffed at sinners. Satan appeared as a woman at the top of a palm tree and Rabbi Akiva started climbing toward her. Halfway up Satan left him, saying heaven's proclamation about Rabbi Akiva and his Torah was all that kept him from ruin.

stories.actor: Peleimu
stories.event: Peleimu used to say daily 'An arrow in Satan's eye,' and on the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came as a repulsive pauper, got himself seated at Peleimu's table and then feigned death.
stories.turn: People cried that Peleimu had killed a man, and he fled and hid in the privy.
stories.outcome: Satan revealed himself, asked why he provoked him, and told him to say instead 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan.'
stories.summary: Peleimu taunted Satan every day. On Yom Kippur eve Satan came as a beggar, pressed to be brought inside and seated at the table, behaved disgustingly, spat into a cup and, when rebuked, collapsed as if dead. Hearing people say he had killed a man, Peleimu fled and hid in the bathroom. Satan followed, revealed himself, and told him to stop his taunt and say 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan' instead.

stories.actor: Mar Yehuda, Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel son of Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Mar Yehuda found the two at the entrance of Rabba's study hall and posed a contradiction between two teachings of Rabbi Shimon.
stories.turn: They fell silent with no answer.
stories.outcome: They went to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome man had put them up to it and resolved the contradiction.
stories.summary: Mar Yehuda came upon Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at the door of Rabba's academy and challenged them with two seemingly contradictory baraitot of Rabbi Shimon on animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard. They had nothing to say. They brought it to Rabba, who dismissed the questioner as quarrelsome and explained the first baraita refers to an animal found to be a tereifa.

stories.actor: A depositor and the family of Rabbi Meyasha
stories.event: A man had deposited seven pearls with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without leaving instructions.
stories.turn: The dispute came before Rabbi Ami.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the depositor, since Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy and the claimant gave identifying marks.
stories.summary: A man left seven pearls wrapped in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who then died without saying whose they were. The depositor and the family came before Rabbi Ami. He ruled for the depositor, since Rabbi Meyasha could not have afforded such pearls and the man identified them.

stories.actor: A depositor and Hasa's household
stories.event: A man had deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The case came before Rav Nahman.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman awarded it to the depositor, because Hasa was not wealthy and the claimant gave a sign.
stories.summary: A silver goblet was deposited with Hasa, who died without explaining it. Before Rav Nahman, the depositor won, since Hasa was known not to be rich and the man described identifying marks.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rav Dimi's household
stories.event: A man had deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The case came before Rabbi Abba.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded the silk to the depositor on the same grounds.
stories.summary: Someone deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without saying so. Rabbi Abba ruled for the depositor, since Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.

stories.actor: A dying man and Toviya
stories.event: A man said on his deathbed that his property should go to Toviya, and after he died a Toviya came to claim it.
stories.turn: There was a question whether this was the intended Toviya.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled 'Toviya has come,' and he received it.
stories.summary: A dying man left his property to 'Toviya.' After his death a man named Toviya appeared. Rabbi Yohanan ruled there was no need to worry about a different Toviya, and gave it to him.

stories.actor: The mother of Rami bar Hama, Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman
stories.event: She deeded her property to Rami bar Hama in the morning and to Mar Ukva bar Hama in the evening, and each son got a different judge to award him the property.
stories.turn: Rav Sheshet confronted Rav Nahman; Rav Nahman rejected his reasoning that the morning deed came first, saying hours are not written outside Jerusalem.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman said he ruled by judicial discretion, and when Rav Sheshet claimed the same, answered that he was a judge and Rav Sheshet was not, and had not reasoned that way to begin with.
stories.summary: Rami bar Hama's mother signed her property to him in the morning and to his brother Mar Ukva that evening. Rav Sheshet awarded it to Rami, and Rav Nahman awarded it to Mar Ukva. When Rav Sheshet challenged him, Rav Nahman dismissed the priority argument since documents do not record hours, and said he had used judges' discretion. Rav Sheshet claimed the same, but Rav Nahman replied that he was the appointed judge and Rav Sheshet was not, and that Rav Sheshet had not ruled on that basis anyway.

stories.actor: Two deed-holders before Rav Yosef
stories.event: Two deeds to one property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just 'Nisan,' and he awarded it to the first.
stories.turn: The other claimant protested that he might have been earlier.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef said he was at a disadvantage since his deed could be from the twenty-ninth; the man then began to ask Rav Yosef to write him something (cut off).
stories.summary: Rav Yosef was shown two deeds for the same land, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one dated only to Nisan, and he gave the land to the holder of the specific date. The other holder asked why he should lose. Rav Yosef answered that his deed might be from the end of the month. The man then started to ask Rav Yosef to write him a document, where the window ends.

stories.actor: Rava
stories.event: At his son's wedding Rava served drinks; Rav Pappa and Rav Huna stood for him but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas did not.
stories.turn: Rava became angry.
stories.outcome: He asked whether the ones who stood were not Sages and those who sat were.
stories.summary: Rava poured drinks for guests at his son's wedding. Two rabbis rose before him and two others stayed seated. Rava was angered and asked sarcastically whether only those who sat counted as Sages.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa
stories.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding and poured for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda.
stories.turn: Rav Yitzhak did not stand for him.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
stories.summary: At his son's wedding Rav Pappa poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, who did not rise before him. Rav Pappa took offense.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
stories.event: At his son's wedding Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, stood serving drinks; Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup but Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it.
stories.turn: Rabbi Eliezer objected that they sit while the Nasi serves them.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, greater still, served guests he took for Arabs, so Rabban Gamliel may serve them (the exchange continues past the window).
stories.summary: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok reclined at Rabban Gamliel's son's wedding while the Nasi himself served drinks. Rabbi Eliezer would not take the cup, but Rabbi Yehoshua did, and Rabbi Eliezer protested. Rabbi Yehoshua replied that Abraham, the greatest of his generation, waited on guests who looked like mere Arabs, so surely Rabban Gamliel may serve them.

stories.actor: A husband and Rabbi Ami
stories.event: A man spent six hundred of his own dinars traveling to collect four hundred his wife inherited, and used one of hers on the way back.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami ruled he could claim nothing, but the Rabbis objected that he had eaten from principal, not produce.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami conceded he could take an oath on his expenses and collect them.
stories.summary: A woman inherited four hundred dinars in distant Bei Hozai, and her husband spent six hundred of his own going to fetch it, taking one dinar of hers on the return trip. Rabbi Ami first ruled that what he spent and what he used were both forfeit. The Rabbis pointed out that he had used principal, not produce, and Rabbi Ami agreed he could swear to his expenses and recover them.

stories.actor: A man and a woman washing her feet
stories.event: A man snatched coins from someone, threw them to a woman washing her feet, and declared her betrothed.
stories.turn: He came before Rava to ask whether the betrothal held.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that nobody accepts Rabbi Shimon's view that the owner despairs, so the coins were stolen and she was not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man grabbed coins from another person and tossed them to a woman who was washing her feet, saying she was betrothed to him. He then asked Rava about it. Rava ruled the money was still stolen and the betrothal was void.

stories.actor: A sharecropper
stories.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field he worked.
stories.turn: He came before Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava asked who had permitted him the onions, ruling them stolen and the betrothal void.
stories.summary: A sharecropper used a handful of onions from his employer's field to betroth a woman. Rava asked him who had given him the onions, meaning they were stolen and she was not betrothed.

stories.actor: A brewer
stories.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with beer sediment belonging to his employer, and the owner found him and suggested he use the sharper sediment.
stories.turn: The brewer asked Rava whether that remark meant the owner had consented.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the 'take the better ones' rule applies only to teruma; the owner spoke from embarrassment, so she was not betrothed.
stories.summary: A brewer making beer for someone betrothed a woman with the sediment. The owner caught him and asked why he hadn't used the better sediment. Rava ruled that such a remark shows consent only in the case of teruma; here the owner was only too embarrassed to protest, so the betrothal failed.

stories.actor: A woman of Mehoza and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A woman from Mehoza married to a man of Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract, and hearing her accent he applied Rav's custom.
stories.turn: They pointed out that she was marrying into Neharde'a.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman reversed and applied Shmuel's custom, that of Neharde'a.
stories.summary: A Mehoza woman married to a Neharde'a man came before Rav Nahman. Recognizing her Mehoza accent, he ruled by Rav's practice followed in Babylonia. When told her husband was from Neharde'a, he ruled instead by Shmuel's practice followed there.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina
stories.event: Dama ben Netina sat among Roman nobles in a golden cloak when his mother came, tore it off, struck his head and spat in his face.
stories.turn: He could have shamed her in return.
stories.outcome: He did not embarrass her.
stories.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Dama ben Netina was once sitting with the nobles of Rome in a gold-embroidered cloak. His mother came, ripped it off him, hit him on the head and spat in his face. He did nothing to humiliate her.

stories.actor: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu
stories.event: Avimi, though ordained with five ordained sons, ran to open the door for his father, and once his father asked for water and dozed off before he brought it.
stories.turn: Avimi stood bent over him until he woke.
stories.outcome: As reward he was helped to expound the psalm 'A song of Asaph.'
stories.summary: Rabbi Abbahu praised his son Avimi for honoring his father: though a scholar with five ordained sons, Avimi would run to open the gate himself, calling 'Yes, yes' as he went. Once Rabbi Abbahu asked for water and fell asleep before Avimi returned, so Avimi stood stooped over him until he woke. In merit of this he succeeded in interpreting the psalm 'A song of Asaph.'

stories.actor: Rabbi Tarfon
stories.event: Rabbi Tarfon would bend down so his mother could step on him into and out of bed, and boasted of it in the study hall.
stories.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached half the honor due.
stories.outcome: They asked whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea before him without his shaming her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon used to bend over so his mother could climb onto and down from her bed by stepping on him. He praised himself for this in the study hall. The Sages told him he had not done even half of what honoring a mother demands, asking whether he had kept silent when she threw his purse into the sea.

stories.actor: A father's heirs and his daughter
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter, but the heirs divided the estate without giving her one.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef thought she had no claim, as in the mishna, but Abaye distinguished the case.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled they must give her a palm tree and redivide the estate.
stories.summary: A man left a palm tree to his daughter in his will, but his sons divided the property and gave her none. Rav Yosef compared it to a case where each party can deflect the claim. Abaye replied that here the tree was held jointly by all of them, so they must give her a tree and divide the estate again.

stories.actor: A father's heirs, his daughter and Rav Ashi
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter but left only two halves of palm trees, which the heirs offered her.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi questioned whether two halves count as a palm tree.
stories.outcome: Rav Mordekhai reported in Rava's name that people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs could give her those.
stories.summary: Another man bequeathed a palm tree to his daughter but died owning only half-shares in two trees. The heirs wanted to give her the two halves. Rav Ashi wondered whether that fulfilled the bequest, and Rav Mordekhai told him that, according to Rava, people do refer to two halves as a palm tree.

stories.actor: Hillel the Elder
stories.event: Hillel provided a poor man of good family with a horse and a servant to run before him.
stories.turn: Once he could not find a servant.
stories.outcome: Hillel himself ran before him for three mil.
stories.summary: Hillel the Elder supplied an impoverished man of noble background with a horse and a servant to run ahead of him. One day no servant was available, so Hillel ran before him himself for three mil.

stories.actor: Rabbi Nehemya and a pauper
stories.event: A poor man asking for charity told Rabbi Nehemya he usually dined on fatty meat and aged wine, and Rabbi Nehemya invited him to share his lentils.
stories.turn: The man ate the lentils and died.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Nehemya lamented 'Woe to this one killed by Nehemya,' meaning the man should not have pampered himself so.
stories.summary: A man came to Rabbi Nehemya for support and said he was used to rich meat and old wine. Rabbi Nehemya asked him to make do with lentils along with him. The man ate them and died, and Rabbi Nehemya said woe to the one killed by Nehemya, blaming the man's indulgence.

stories.actor: Rava and a pauper
stories.event: A poor man told Rava he dined on fattened hen and aged wine and, rebuked for burdening the community, said he ate from God, who gives each his food.
stories.turn: Just then Rava's sister, unseen for thirteen years, arrived bringing fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.outcome: Rava saw it as a sign, apologized and told the man to sit and eat.
stories.summary: A man seeking charity told Rava he was accustomed to fattened chicken and aged wine. Rava asked whether he cared about the strain on the community, and the man answered that God provides each person's food. At that moment Rava's sister, whom he had not seen in thirteen years, arrived with exactly those foods. Rava conceded the point and invited the man to eat.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
stories.event: Heirs claimed a bag of documents deposited with her, and she said she seized it from the deceased in his lifetime.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that he had demanded it and she refused; she had none.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled it a seizure after death, which is void.
stories.summary: A woman held a bag of documents and the heirs demanded it, but she said she had taken it before the owner died against his debt. Rav Nahman asked for witnesses; she had none. He ruled her seizure counted as after death and was ineffective.

stories.actor: Rava and Rav Hisda's daughter
stories.event: A woman was obligated to swear in Rava's court.
stories.turn: Rav Hisda's daughter told Rava the woman was suspected of false oaths.
stories.outcome: Rava reversed the oath onto the opposing party.
stories.summary: A woman owed an oath in Rava's court. Rava's wife told him the woman was known to swear falsely. Rava turned the oath over to the other side.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa, Rav Adda bar Mattana and Rava
stories.event: Rav Pappa testified to Rava that a document before the court had been paid.
stories.turn: Rava refused one witness, and Rav Adda bar Mattana asked why Rav Pappa was not trusted like Rav Hisda's daughter.
stories.outcome: Rava said he was certain of her truthfulness but not of Rav Pappa's.
stories.summary: While Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana sat before Rava, a document was brought and Rav Pappa said it had been paid. Rava said a lone witness counts for nothing. Challenged by Rav Adda, Rava explained he trusted his wife's word from certain knowledge but had no such certainty about Rav Pappa.

stories.actor: A woman in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court
stories.event: A woman was obligated to swear, and her opponent asked that she swear publicly in town in hopes she would be shamed into confessing.
stories.turn: She demanded a written document of her rights so she would be paid once she swore.
stories.outcome: Rav Beivai bar Abaye ordered the document written for her.
stories.summary: A woman had to take an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court. Her opponent asked that she swear in the town, hoping embarrassment would make her admit the truth. She agreed on condition she receive a written record of her rights, and Rav Beivai told the court to write it.

stories.actor: A man of Shihin
stories.event: A man inherited three mustard stalks from his father, and one broke.
stories.turn: Nine kav of mustard were found on that single stalk.
stories.outcome: Its wood was used to roof a potters' booth.
stories.summary: In Shihin a man's father left him three mustard stalks. When one broke, it turned out to hold nine kav of mustard seed, and its wood was big enough to roof an artisans' booth.

stories.actor: Aher (Elisha ben Avuya)
stories.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator, executed by the government, being dragged by a pig (or, some say, saw a son die after fulfilling a mitzva).
stories.turn: He exclaimed, 'Shall a mouth that produced pearls lick dust?'
stories.outcome: He went out and sinned.
stories.summary: The Gemara asks what led Elisha ben Avuya astray. Some say he saw a son die after performing a mitzva his father commanded. Others say he saw the tongue of the executed sage Hutzpit dragged through the street by a pig and cried out that a mouth that produced pearls should not lick dust, and then abandoned the faith and sinned.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, so he used an incantation to cover himself with boils, but she healed him by magic.
stories.turn: He fled and hid in a bathhouse so dangerous that even two people entering by day were harmed.
stories.outcome: He survived the night, guarded, he said, by two imperial guards; the Sages explained a miracle is done for one who escapes forbidden intercourse.
stories.summary: A noblewoman pressed Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi to sleep with her. He made himself repulsive with boils through an incantation, but she cured him with magic, so he fled into a demon-haunted bathhouse. The next day the Sages asked who had protected him, and he said two imperial soldiers guarded him all night. They concluded that he had resisted a sexual temptation, and that a miracle is performed for such a person.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael
stories.event: Rabbi Yishmael had two scholars judge a case of a sharecropper who had brought him fruits, and found himself mentally arguing the litigant's side.
stories.turn: He realized that even without taking a bribe he was biased.
stories.outcome: He cursed those who take bribes, concluding they are surely far more biased.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael recused himself and seated two scholars to judge the case. As he walked about he kept thinking of arguments for the man who had brought him the fruit. He exclaimed that if he, who took nothing that was not his, was so swayed, how much more so are those who take bribes.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha
stories.event: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing from far away.
stories.turn: Questioned, the man admitted he had a case to bring before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift, recused himself, and found himself biased in the man's favor anyway, cursing bribe-takers.
stories.summary: A man came from a distant place to give the priest Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing. When asked why he had not given it to a nearer priest, he said he had a case before him. Rabbi Yishmael declared himself disqualified, refused the gift and had two scholars judge it, yet still caught himself thinking of the man's arguments, and concluded how much more biased real bribe-takers must be.

stories.actor: Rav Anan
stories.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of fish; Rav Anan refused it as he had a case, but accepted it after the man said he wanted to honor a scholar, and referred the case to Rav Nahman.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman assumed the man was Rav Anan's relative, gave him precedence and honor, and the opposing litigant was intimidated and lost.
stories.outcome: Elijah stopped visiting Rav Anan; after fasting and prayer Elijah returned but frightened him, so Rav Anan sat in a box to learn, producing the two Orders of Elijah.
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan fish; Rav Anan refused because the man had a case, but when the man said he wanted to fulfill the mitzva of giving a gift to a scholar, he accepted it and sent the man with a letter to Rav Nahman, saying he was disqualified. Rav Nahman took him for a relative of Rav Anan, put aside an orphans' case and honored him, so his opponent was cowed and lost. Elijah, who had been teaching Rav Anan, stopped coming; Rav Anan fasted and Elijah returned, but now frightened him, so Rav Anan sat in a box before him, which is why there is a Major and a Minor Seder Eliyahu.

stories.actor: A wife who brought two maidservants into her marriage
stories.event: Her husband married a second wife and gave one of the first wife's maidservants to the second.
stories.turn: She cried out before Rava about the injustice.
stories.outcome: Rava ignored her complaint.
stories.summary: A woman brought two maidservants into her marriage. Her husband married another woman and assigned one of the maidservants to her. The first wife came crying to Rava, but he paid no attention to her.

stories.actor: A glass-bead seller and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string, and he asked whether she would be betrothed to him with it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give, give'.
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that such a reply means nothing; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was selling glass beads, and a woman asked him for a string. He asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it to her, and she said, 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that this mocking reply is nothing.

stories.actor: A man drinking wine and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man drinking in a shop for a cup, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him with it.
stories.turn: She said 'Give me to drink, give me to drink'.
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that this reply is nothing.
stories.summary: A woman asked a man drinking in a shop for a cup of wine. He asked if she would be betrothed to him with it, and she said, 'Pour, pour me a drink.' Rav Hama ruled she was not betrothed.

stories.actor: A man picking dates and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man picking dates to throw her two, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him with them.
stories.turn: She said 'Throw, throw'.
stories.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled that this reply is nothing.
stories.summary: A man was knocking dates off a palm, and a woman asked him to throw her two. He asked if she would be betrothed to him with them, and she said, 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled she was not betrothed.

stories.actor: A certain widow
stories.event: A woman visiting her husband's grave had relations with a guard of an executed man's body.
stories.turn: The body he guarded was taken.
stories.outcome: She removed her husband's body from the grave so the guard could substitute it.
stories.summary: A mourning widow at her husband's grave was seduced by a man guarding the body of someone the king had executed. When that body was stolen, she had her husband disinterred so the guard could put it in its place. The incident shows temptation persists even in mourning.

stories.actor: A belt seller and a man
stories.event: A man snatched a belt from a woman selling belts and asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it back.
stories.turn: She took it and remained silent.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled she could claim she was merely taking back her own property, so she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A woman was selling belts when a man grabbed one. When she demanded it back, he asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he returned it; she took it silently. Rav Nahman ruled she could say she was only taking what was hers.

stories.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
stories.event: Rav Aha spent the night in a study hall haunted by a demon.
stories.turn: The demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent, and with each bow of his prayer a head fell off.
stories.outcome: The demon died, and the next day he rebuked the townspeople for endangering him.
stories.summary: Rav Aha slept in the study hall where a demon lurked. It appeared to him as a seven-headed serpent, and each time he bowed in prayer one head fell off. The next morning he told the townspeople that without a miracle they would have endangered him.

stories.actor: Rav Huna and Rav Hamnuna
stories.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna, so Rav Huna asked to meet him.
stories.turn: Rav Huna saw he wore no head covering and learned it was because he was unmarried.
stories.outcome: Rav Huna turned away and told him not to see his face until he married.
stories.summary: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked to have him sent over. When he came, Rav Huna noticed he did not cover his head, and Rav Hamnuna explained he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to come before him until he married.

stories.actor: Rav Rehumi and his wife
stories.event: Rav Rehumi, who came home every Yom Kippur eve, stayed engrossed in study one year.
stories.turn: His waiting wife was distressed and shed a tear.
stories.outcome: The roof he was sitting on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi studied with Rava in Mehoza and always came home on the eve of Yom Kippur. One year he became absorbed in study and did not come; his wife kept expecting him and finally shed a tear. At that moment the roof under him collapsed and he died.

stories.actor: Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Yehuda came home every Friday at twilight, preceded by a pillar of fire seen by his father-in-law Rabbi Yannai.
stories.turn: One week he stayed at study, and Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared he must be dead.
stories.outcome: The words acted like a ruler's error and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya studied all week and returned home every Shabbat eve, with a pillar of fire going before him. One week he stayed late at study, and Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the fire, said to overturn his bed since he must have died. His statement came true and Yehuda died.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
stories.event: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's family.
stories.turn: The bride died when the marriage contract was about to be written.
stories.outcome: Investigating, they found a genealogical mismatch: Rabbi descended from David's wife, Rabbi Hiyya from David's brother.
stories.summary: Rabbi arranged a match for his son with a daughter of Rabbi Hiyya's household, but the girl died just as the ketuba was to be written. Rabbi wondered if there was some flaw in the families. Examining the lineage, they found Rabbi descended from Shefatya ben Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from Shimi, David's brother.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son
stories.event: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: On seeing the bride, the son reduced it to six years, then decided to marry first.
stories.outcome: Ashamed before his father, he was reassured that he acted as God did, citing verses; the story continues past the window.
stories.summary: Rabbi then arranged a match with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, who agreed to support the groom for twelve years of study. When the bride was shown to him he asked for six years, and when shown again said he would marry first and then study. He was ashamed before his father, who told him he had his Maker's insight, as God too advanced His plan to dwell among Israel.

stories.actor: Rav Rehumi and his wife
stories.event: Rav Rehumi, who came home every Yom Kippur eve, stayed engrossed in study one year.
stories.turn: His waiting wife was distressed and shed a tear.
stories.outcome: The roof he was sitting on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi studied with Rava and always returned home on the eve of Yom Kippur. One year he stayed absorbed in study; his wife waited and finally shed a tear. The roof beneath him collapsed and he died.

stories.actor: Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Yehuda came home every Friday at twilight, preceded by a pillar of fire seen by Rabbi Yannai.
stories.turn: One week he stayed at study, and Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared him dead.
stories.outcome: The statement came true and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya came home each Shabbat eve with a pillar of fire before him. One week he stayed at study, and Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the fire, ordered his bed overturned as for a mourner. Like an error from a ruler, it came true and Yehuda died.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
stories.event: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's family.
stories.turn: The bride died as the marriage contract was being written.
stories.outcome: They found a genealogical mismatch between the families.
stories.summary: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry a girl of Rabbi Hiyya's household, but she died as the ketuba was about to be written. Suspecting a flaw, they examined the lineage. Rabbi descended from Shefatya ben Avital, while Rabbi Hiyya descended from Shimi, David's brother.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son
stories.event: Rabbi's son was matched with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter on condition of twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: Seeing her, he chose to marry first; after twelve years away she became infertile.
stories.outcome: Rabbi weighed divorce or a second wife, and instead the husband prayed for her and she was healed.
stories.summary: Rabbi's son was to study twelve years before marrying a daughter of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, but on seeing her he reduced it to six and then married her first; his father reassured him he had acted like God. He then studied twelve years away, and returned to find his wife infertile. Rabbi rejected both divorce and a second wife as unjust to her, so the husband prayed and she was cured.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai
stories.event: Rabbi Hananya left for the study hall at the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast, refusing to wait for him.
stories.turn: He stayed twelve years.
stories.outcome: When he returned, the town's paths had changed and he could not find his way home; the story continues past the window.
stories.summary: At the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding celebration, Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai set off for the study hall. Rabbi Shimon asked him to wait so they could go together, but he did not. He studied for twelve years, and by the time he came back the streets had changed and he did not know the way to his house.

stories.actor: Ilfa
stories.event: Ilfa hung himself from a ship's mast, vowing to fall and drown if anyone cited a baraita he could not derive from a mishna.
stories.turn: An old man challenged him with a baraita about a dying man's instructions to give his sons a shekel weekly.
stories.outcome: Ilfa identified it as following Rabbi Meir's view in the mishna and met the challenge.
stories.summary: Passed over for head of the academy, Ilfa suspended himself from a ship's mast and declared he would drop into the sea if anyone brought a teaching of the school of Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya that he could not trace to a mishna. An old man cited a baraita on a father's deathbed allowance for his sons. Ilfa answered that it follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one must fulfill the instructions of the dead, and so he succeeded.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya Arikha and his mother-in-law
stories.event: Rav Hiyya supported his brother's widow for twenty-five years in her father's house, then refused her further sustenance and her ketuba.
