stories.turn: Rabba bar Sheila ruled for her and wrote an authorization to seize his property, which Rava upheld.
stories.outcome: When she then claimed the produce, Rava found the authorization defectively written and denied her the produce.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya Arikha supported his widowed sister-in-law, who was also his mother-in-law, for twenty-five years, but then refused her both sustenance and her ketuba. She sued before Rabba bar Sheila, who ruled she had not claimed only out of embarrassment and ordered payment; when Rav Hiyya ignored him he authorized her to seize his property, and Rava said the ruling was good. But when she asked Rava for the produce since then, he examined the document, found it lacked the statement that the property was the deceased's, and ruled it defective, rejecting all her counter-arguments.

stories.actor: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan
stories.event: Walking outside Eretz Yisrael, they saw men sowing mixed seeds, and one proposed excommunicating them.
stories.turn: The other said he misunderstood the law.
stories.outcome: Both times the other refused, explaining these plantings were not forbidden there.
stories.summary: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan were traveling and saw a man sowing mixed seeds; one suggested they ostracize him, but the other said he did not understand these laws. They then saw a man sowing wheat and barley among vines, and again one wanted to ostracize him. The other explained that by Rabbi Yoshiya's view this is not liable unless sown together in one hand motion.

stories.actor: Rav and Rav Yehuda
stories.event: Walking on the road with a woman ahead of them, Rav told Rav Yehuda to hurry away from Gehenna.
stories.turn: Rav Yehuda objected that Rav himself permitted it for men of fit morals.
stories.outcome: Rav replied that he meant men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, not themselves.
stories.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were on the road behind a woman, and Rav urged Rav Yehuda to walk quickly away from her. Rav Yehuda reminded him that he had ruled such seclusion permitted for upright men. Rav answered that he did not mean people like them, but men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.

stories.actor: Rav Amram
stories.event: Rav Amram was climbing a ladder toward a woman when he stopped himself halfway.
stories.turn: He cried out 'Fire in Amram's house', bringing the Sages, and accepted their shame over shame in the World to Come.
stories.outcome: He adjured his evil inclination to leave him; it emerged as a pillar of fire, and he declared himself its master.
stories.summary: Halfway up the ladder, Rav Amram braced himself and shouted that there was a fire in his house. The Sages came and said he had embarrassed them, but he said better to be ashamed now than in the World to Come. He made his evil inclination leave him; it came out like a pillar of fire, and he told it that though it was fire and he only flesh, he was stronger.

stories.actor: Rabbi Meir
stories.event: Rabbi Meir mocked transgressors, and Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river.
stories.turn: He began crossing on a rope bridge toward her.
stories.outcome: Halfway across, Satan left him, saying only Heaven's warning to protect him had spared him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman on the other side of a river, and with no ferry he started across a rope bridge. Halfway over, Satan let him go and said that were it not for Heaven's proclamation to protect Rabbi Meir, his life would have been worthless.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva
stories.event: Rabbi Akiva mocked transgressors, and Satan appeared to him as a woman atop a palm tree.
stories.turn: He began climbing the tree.
stories.outcome: Halfway up, Satan left him, saying only Heaven's warning had spared him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also scoffed at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and he began to climb. Halfway up Satan released him, saying that only Heaven's proclamation protecting him had saved him.

stories.actor: Peleimu
stories.event: Peleimu, who daily cursed Satan, received Satan disguised as a repulsive pauper on Yom Kippur eve.
stories.turn: The pauper pretended to die after being rebuked, and people cried that Peleimu had killed a man.
stories.outcome: Peleimu hid in the outhouse; Satan revealed himself and told him to say instead 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan'.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to say every day, 'An arrow in Satan's eye.' On the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came as a pauper, demanded to be brought inside and seated at the table, then behaved disgustingly and spat into a cup; when rebuked he collapsed as if dead, and people shouted that Peleimu had killed a man. Peleimu fled and hid, and when Satan saw his distress he revealed himself and told him to say, 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan.'

stories.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi and his wife
stories.event: His wife, puzzled by his prayer against the evil inclination though he had long withdrawn from her, disguised herself as the prostitute Haruta.
stories.turn: He propositioned her and they had relations; at home he confessed, and she revealed it was she.
stories.outcome: He said he had intended to sin, and fasted the rest of his life until he died of it.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi prayed daily to be saved from the evil inclination, which puzzled his wife since he had abstained from her for years. She adorned herself and passed him in his garden as Haruta the prostitute; he propositioned her and fetched her a pomegranate as payment. At home he sat in the lit oven in remorse; she proved it had been her, but he said he had still meant to sin, and fasted until he died.

stories.actor: Rava
stories.event: Rava served drinks at his son's wedding.
stories.turn: Two Sages stood for him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas did not.
stories.outcome: Rava became angry and rebuked them.
stories.summary: At his son's wedding Rava poured drinks for the guests. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua rose before him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda did not. Rava was angered and asked whether only they were Sages and the others not.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa
stories.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding.
stories.turn: Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda did not stand for him.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa poured drinks at the wedding of his son Abba Mar. When he poured for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, the latter did not rise before him. Rav Pappa was offended.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel and his guests
stories.event: Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, stood serving drinks at his son's wedding.
stories.turn: Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup and objected when Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua cited Abraham serving guests and Rabbi Tzadok cited God's providing for all, justifying it.
stories.summary: At Rabban Gamliel's son's wedding, the Nasi himself stood and poured for Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok. Rabbi Eliezer would not take the cup and rebuked Rabbi Yehoshua for accepting it. Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, greater still, served guests he took for Arabs, and Rabbi Tzadok added that God Himself sets a table for every creature.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa and a seller
stories.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money for oxen.
stories.turn: In the end he did not need the money.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land to him, beyond the letter of the law.
stories.summary: A man sold Rav Pappa a field to raise money to buy oxen. In the end he did not need it. Rav Pappa gave him back his land, acting beyond what the law required.

stories.actor: The people of Neharde'a and Rav Nahman
stories.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
stories.turn: Wheat arrived, and it emerged the ship had already been near when they sold.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled the mansions return to their owners, defending the ruling to Rami bar Shmuel.
stories.summary: In a famine in Neharde'a people sold their mansions to buy wheat, but then wheat arrived. Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions go back to their owners, since the ship was already in the river bends at the time of sale. Rami bar Shmuel objected that this would discourage buyers, and Rav Nahman replied droughts are not daily, to which Rami said in Neharde'a they are frequent.

stories.actor: Rav Anan
stories.event: A man gave Rav Anan a gift as a scholar; Rav Anan accepted it and referred his case to Rav Nahman, saying he was disqualified.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman assumed the man was Rav Anan's relative and favored him, so his opponent was intimidated and lost.
stories.outcome: Elijah stopped visiting Rav Anan, then returned after his fast but frightened him, so he learned sitting in a box, producing the two Orders of Elijah.
stories.summary: The man told Rav Anan he wanted him to accept the gift as one brings first fruits; Rav Anan accepted and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note that he was disqualified. Rav Nahman took the man for Rav Anan's relative, put aside an orphans' case to hear his, and the honor shown silenced the opposing litigant. Elijah, who had been teaching Rav Anan, left him; after fasting Elijah returned but frightened him, so Rav Anan sat in a box to learn, hence Seder Eliyahu Rabba and Zuta.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
stories.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing his grandchild to the synagogue with only a cheap cloth on his head.
stories.turn: Asked why, he cited the verse linking teaching grandchildren to standing at Sinai.
stories.outcome: From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat breakfast before teaching his child.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying a child to the synagogue, hastily wrapped in a simple head covering. He asked what the rush was, and Rabbi Yehoshua answered that teaching one's grandchildren is likened to receiving the Torah at Horeb. After that Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba never ate breakfast before reviewing with his child and adding to his lesson.

stories.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of bar Elyashiv
stories.event: A widow claiming her ketuba from the orphans was told by them to dress properly for court.
stories.turn: She put on all her clothes.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled with Rav that a widow's clothes on her are appraised toward her ketuba.
stories.summary: A widow of the bar Elyashiv family was taking the orphans to court for her ketuba. They said it shamed them for her to go in house clothes, so she dressed in all her garments. Ravina ruled, following Rav, that whatever she is wearing is appraised and deducted from her ketuba.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives and their stepmother
stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, burdened by their stepmother's spending, were advised by him to have their father set aside land for her sustenance.
stories.turn: After the father died, Reish Lakish ruled the land only added to her support and threatened them when they cited Rabbi Yohanan.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan told them he could do nothing since an equal disagreed with him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives complained that their father's wife was squandering his money on her upkeep, and he advised them to have their father allot her a field for sustenance. After their father died, Reish Lakish ruled that this only increased what she could draw and threatened them harshly when they cited Rabbi Yohanan. They complained to Rabbi Yohanan, who said he could do nothing, since a colleague of equal standing disagreed.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: At his death the Angel of Death was sent to do his bidding, and he asked to see his place in paradise and to hold the angel's knife.
stories.turn: Shown his place, he jumped into paradise and swore not to leave.
stories.outcome: God let him stay since he never annulled an oath; he returned the knife at a Divine Voice's command, and met Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai there.
stories.summary: When Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was dying, the Angel of Death was told to grant his wishes; he asked to see his place in paradise and to hold the knife so he would not be frightened. When lifted to see it, he leapt over into paradise and swore he would not come back; God ruled that since he had never had an oath annulled he could stay, and a Divine Voice made him return the knife. Elijah announced him, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai questioned him about whether a rainbow had appeared in his lifetime.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa
stories.event: When dying, Rabbi Hanina asked the Angel of Death for thirty days to review his learning, then for the knife.
stories.turn: The angel refused, suspecting the same trick as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
stories.outcome: At his death a pillar of fire separated him from everyone, and it withdrew only when Rabbi Alexandri appealed to his own honor.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa, a friend of the Angel of Death, asked for thirty days to review his studies, then asked to see his place and to hold the knife. The angel refused, asking if he meant to repeat Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's trick, and dismissed his claim of having kept the whole Torah since he had not tended the afflicted. When he died a pillar of fire surrounded him, and it lifted only when Rabbi Alexandri asked him to remove it for his own honor.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his yearly 400 dinars to a poor neighbor through his son.
stories.turn: The son reported the man did not need it, since they spilled old wine for him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva decided the man was so pampered he needed more, doubled the money and sent it.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to send a poor neighbor 400 dinars every Yom Kippur eve. Once his son brought it and came back saying the man did not need it, because he saw them spilling old wine for him. Mar Ukva said that if he is that pampered he needs more, and doubled the gift.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records.
stories.turn: He saw he had given seven thousand gold dinars and judged it too little for the long road ahead.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his remaining wealth to charity.
stories.summary: As Mar Ukva was dying he asked for his charity accounts and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the journey long, he gave away half his money. The Gemara then explains why this did not violate the one-fifth limit.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina and his wife
stories.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his weekly four dinars to a poor man through his wife.
stories.turn: She heard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths and said he did not need charity.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responded by citing Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent a poor man four dinars before Shabbat. Once his wife delivered it and returned saying the man did not need it, since she heard them ask whether he would dine on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina replied with Rabbi Elazar's saying that swindlers deserve thanks, since without them we would sin daily by neglecting the poor.

stories.actor: A bead seller and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him with it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give, give.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that 'give, give' means nothing; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man selling glass beads was asked by a woman for a string. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she said 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that such an answer is mockery and creates no betrothal.

stories.actor: A man drinking wine and a woman
stories.event: A woman in a wine shop asked a man for a cup, and he asked if she would be betrothed with it.
stories.turn: She replied 'Give me to drink, give me to drink.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled the reply means nothing and she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man drinking in a store was asked by a woman for a cup of wine. He asked if she would be betrothed to him by it, and she answered 'Give me to drink.' Rav Hama ruled that this answer does not effect betrothal.

stories.actor: A date picker and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man picking dates to throw her two, and he asked if she would be betrothed with them.
stories.turn: She said 'Throw, throw.'
stories.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled that this means nothing and she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was picking dates when a woman asked him to throw her two. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him by them, and she said 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that this is not acceptance and she is not betrothed.

stories.actor: A maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household
stories.event: The maidservant immersed and came out of the ritual bath.
stories.turn: A bone was found between her teeth.
stories.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again.
stories.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household immersed herself, and after she came up a bone was found stuck between her teeth. Rabbi ruled the immersion invalid and required her to immerse again.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Three Sages visiting a place were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot.
stories.turn: A year later Rabbi Elazar came and was given a peach small enough to hold in one hand.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Elazar quoted the verse that a fruitful land becomes salt waste because of its inhabitants' wickedness.
stories.summary: Three Sages came to a certain place and were served an enormous peach; they ate a third, left a third ownerless, and fed a third to their animals. The next year Rabbi Elazar visited and the peach fit in his hand. He cited Psalms: a fruitful land turns to salt waste for the wickedness of its people.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw grape clusters in Gavla as large as calves.
stories.turn: He told the earth to withhold its fruit from the gentiles who ruled them, and the next year the clusters were only the size of goats.
stories.outcome: When Rabbi Hiyya remarked on them, the locals told him to leave and not do what his colleague had done.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi came to Gavla and mistook grape clusters for calves among the vines. Told they were grapes, he called on the earth to gather in its fruit rather than produce it for the gentile rulers. The next year Rabbi Hiyya found clusters the size of goats, and the locals told him to go away and not curse them as his colleague had.

stories.actor: A blind man who studied with Mar Shmuel
stories.event: The blind man was late, so Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to his house, who missed him on the way.
stories.turn: The messenger returned and reported that the blind man's wife had committed adultery.
stories.outcome: Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not otherwise.
stories.summary: A blind man who recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel was late one day, and Mar Shmuel sent a messenger after him. They passed each other, the messenger reached the house and came back saying the man's wife had committed adultery. Mar Shmuel told the blind man to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and otherwise not to.

stories.actor: King Yannai and Elazar ben Po'ira
stories.event: After conquering sixty cities, King Yannai feasted the Sages on salty food from golden tables.
stories.turn: Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees secretly opposed him and advised testing them with the High Priest's frontplate.
stories.outcome: Yannai stood the Pharisees before him wearing the frontplate (the story continues past the window).
stories.summary: King Yannai returned joyful from conquering sixty cities in Kohalit and summoned the Sages to eat salty foods on golden tables in memory of their ancestors. A scoundrel named Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees' hearts were against him and suggested he wear the frontplate before them. Yannai did so; the story continues beyond the window.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: The two Sages seized a dead debtor's boat for themselves and each claimed to have acquired all of it.
stories.turn: Rav Pinehas bar Ami challenged them, and they took the case to Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava rebuked them as white geese stealing cloaks, since seizure after the debtor's death is invalid.
stories.summary: Having told another man's agent his seizure was invalid, Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua seized the boat themselves, one rowing and one pulling, each claiming the whole. Rav Pinehas bar Ami objected that seized goods must lie in the public domain, and they answered they took it from midstream. Rava rebuked them, ruling that seizure counts only while the debtor is alive.

stories.actor: Hama son of Rabba bar Abbahu
stories.event: Hama paid Avimi's debt to the people of Bei Hozai and asked for the loan document back.
stories.turn: They claimed the money was for other, undocumented debts.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu ruled that without witnesses to the payment they could keep both money and document.
stories.summary: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu sent money to his creditors in Bei Hozai through Hama son of Rabba bar Abbahu. After paying, Hama asked for the document, but they said the money covered side debts. Rabbi Abbahu asked whether he had witnesses to the payment; he had none, so the creditors' claim stood.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
stories.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents that had been deposited with a woman.
stories.turn: She claimed she had seized it during the deceased's lifetime for a debt, but had no witnesses.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled it was a seizure after death, which is void.
stories.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and the heirs came to claim it. She said she had seized it while the owner was alive because he owed her money. Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that he demanded it in his lifetime and she refused; she had none, so he ruled the seizure was after death and invalid.

stories.actor: A son sent by his father to fetch chicks
stories.event: At his father's request a son climbed a building, sent away the mother bird and took the chicks.
stories.turn: On his way down he fell.
stories.outcome: He died, despite fulfilling two mitzvot promising long life.
stories.summary: A father told his son to climb up and bring him chicks. The son climbed, sent away the mother bird and took the young, fulfilling both mitzvot whose reward is long life, but fell on his return and died. Rabbi Ya'akov uses this incident to argue the reward refers to the World-to-Come.

stories.actor: Aher (Elisha ben Avuya)
stories.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator dragged in the street by a pig.
stories.turn: He exclaimed: shall a mouth that produced pearls lick the dust?
stories.outcome: He went out and sinned.
stories.summary: Rav Yosef says Aher would not have sinned had he read the verse as Rabbi Ya'akov did; some say he saw a son die after sending away the mother bird. Others say he saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged by a pig. He cried that a mouth that produced pearls now licks dust, and went out and sinned.

stories.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
stories.event: Rav Aha found his son's studies weak and went to study with Abaye himself.
stories.turn: Abaye had the townspeople refuse him lodging so he would sleep in the study hall haunted by a demon.
stories.outcome: The demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent; each time Rav Aha bowed in prayer a head fell off, and he survived.
stories.summary: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov sent his son to Abaye, but on his return saw his learning was not sharp, so he decided to go himself. Abaye, hoping for a miracle against a dangerous demon in his study hall, told the townspeople not to host him. Rav Aha slept there, the demon came as a seven-headed serpent, and with each bow of his prayer a head fell off. The next day he told them they had endangered him.

stories.actor: Rav Hamnuna and Rav Huna
stories.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna, and Rav Huna asked to meet him.
stories.turn: Rav Huna saw he did not cover his head and learned it was because he was unmarried.
stories.outcome: Rav Huna turned away and told him not to see his face again until he married.
stories.summary: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked to meet him. When Rav Hamnuna came without a head covering, he explained he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to appear before him until he married.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Three Sages visiting a place were served an enormous peach.
stories.turn: A year later Rabbi Elazar was given a peach that fit in his hand.
stories.outcome: He quoted the verse that a fruitful land becomes salt waste through its inhabitants' wickedness.
stories.summary: Three Sages came to a certain place and were served a peach the size of a five-se'a stewpot, which they divided among themselves, the public, and their animals. A year later Rabbi Elazar came and the peach was small enough to hold. He cited the verse about a fruitful land turned to salt waste for its people's sins.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw grape clusters in Gavla as big as calves.
stories.turn: He told the earth to withhold its fruit from the gentile rulers, and the clusters shrank to the size of goats.
stories.outcome: When Rabbi Hiyya came the next year, the locals told him to leave and not do as his colleague had.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi visited Gavla and mistook huge grape clusters for calves. He told the land to stop producing fruit for the gentiles who ruled over them. The next year Rabbi Hiyya saw clusters like goats, and the locals sent him away so he would not curse them too.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina
stories.event: A red heifer was born in Dama ben Netina's herd as a reward for honoring his father.
stories.turn: The Sages came to buy it, ready to pay any price.
stories.outcome: He asked only for the money he had lost by honoring his father.
stories.summary: The year after Dama ben Netina gave up a profit to honor his father, a red heifer was born in his herd. When the Sages came to buy it, he said he knew they would pay anything. He asked only for the sum he had lost for his father's honor.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina and his mother
stories.event: Dama ben Netina sat among the nobles of Rome in a golden cloak.
stories.turn: His mother came, tore the cloak off him, struck his head and spat in his face.
stories.outcome: He did not shame her.
stories.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Dama ben Netina once sat among Rome's nobles wearing a gold cloak. His mother came, tore it from him, hit him on the head and spat in his face. Still he did not embarrass her.

stories.actor: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu
stories.event: Avimi, though ordained and with five ordained sons, personally ran to open the door for his father.
stories.turn: Whenever Rabbi Abbahu called at the gate, Avimi called out 'Yes, yes' as he ran.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu held him up as one who properly fulfilled honoring parents (account continues past the window).
stories.summary: Rabbi Abbahu said his son Avimi fulfilled the mitzva of honoring parents. Though Avimi had five ordained sons, when his father called at the gate he ran to open it himself, calling 'Yes, yes' on the way so his father would not feel ignored.

stories.actor: Ravin the Pious
stories.event: Ravin went to betroth a woman to his son.
stories.turn: Her family would not give her to the son, only to him.
stories.outcome: He betrothed her to himself without first telling his son, fearing someone else would take her.
stories.summary: Ravin the Pious went as an agent to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her to himself. The Gemara explains that her family refused the son and would only give her to Ravin. He did not stop to inform his son because someone else might have betrothed her in the meantime.

stories.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a field for him.
stories.turn: Rav bought it for himself instead.
stories.outcome: The Gemara explains that the violent locals would sell only to Rav, and he feared losing it if he delayed.
stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a certain field for him, but Rav bought it for himself. The field lay among violent men who respected Rav and not Rabba bar bar Hana. Rav did not tell him first, fearing that someone else would buy it meanwhile.

stories.actor: Rav Giddel and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: Rabbi Abba bought a field Rav Giddel had been negotiating for.
stories.turn: Rav Yitzhak Nappaha confronted Rabbi Abba, who said he had not known and offered it as a gift since he would not sell his first land.
stories.outcome: Rav Giddel refused the gift and Rabbi Abba would not use it, so it became known as the land of the Sages.
stories.summary: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a field when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, and at the Festival he asked Rabbi Abba what happens when someone snatches a pauper's loaf. Rabbi Abba said he had not known and offered the field as a gift, since selling a first purchase is a bad omen. Rav Giddel would not take gifts and Rabbi Abba would not use it, so it was called the land of the Sages.

stories.actor: The family of the woman betrothed with a blue marble stone
stories.event: The family descended from that woman's later marriage remained in Sura.
stories.turn: The Sages suspected the first betrothal might have been valid.
stories.outcome: The Sages refused to marry into the family.
stories.summary: After Rav Hisda invalidated a betrothal made with a blue marble stone, the woman married another man and had descendants in Sura. The Sages kept away from that family, out of concern the children might be mamzerim, following Abaye and Rava's view.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed with a myrtle branch
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman in the marketplace with a myrtle branch.
stories.turn: Rav Aha bar Huna sent the case to Rav Yosef.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled to flog the man and require a divorce.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman in the market with a myrtle branch. Rav Aha bar Huna asked Rav Yosef what to do. Rav Yosef replied to flog him as Rav would, and require a bill of divorce as Shmuel would, in case the branch was worth a peruta elsewhere.

stories.actor: A son-in-law and Rav Sheshet
stories.event: A son-in-law passed by the door of his father-in-law's house.
stories.turn: There were rumors about him and his mother-in-law.
stories.outcome: Rav Sheshet had him flogged.
stories.summary: A certain son-in-law walked past his father-in-law's door, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The Gemara explains that there were suspicions of intimacy between him and his mother-in-law, which his passing fed.

stories.actor: A herdsman of orphans and a creditor
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman.
stories.turn: The creditor said he seized it in the father's lifetime; the herdsman said after his death; there were no witnesses.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the creditor, since he could have claimed he bought it.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman of some orphans. The creditor said he seized it while their father was alive, and the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman found the herdsman had no witnesses and ruled for the creditor, who could as easily have claimed he bought it.

stories.actor: The house of the Nasi and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: The Nasi's household seized a maidservant of orphans in an alley for a debt.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abbahu approved, but Rabbi Abba accused the judges of flattering the Nasi.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba cited that Reish Lakish reversed such a ruling (window does not say how it ended).
stories.summary: Members of the Nasi's house seized an orphans' maidservant in an alley as payment of their father's debt. Rabbi Abbahu, judging with colleagues, said they had seized well. Rabbi Abba rebuked them for currying favor with the Nasi, noting Reish Lakish had overturned a similar ruling.

stories.actor: Yeimar bar Hashu, Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: Yeimar's agent seized a dead debtor's boat.
stories.turn: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna told him the seizure was invalid and took the boat themselves, each claiming all of it.
stories.outcome: Rava rebuked them as white geese stealing cloaks, since seizure after death does not count.
stories.summary: Yeimar bar Hashu sent his agent to seize a boat left by a debtor who had died. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua told the agent he could not seize to the detriment of other creditors, then seized it themselves, each claiming the whole. When Rav Pinehas bar Ami objected they said they took it from midstream. Rava called them white geese who strip people's cloaks, since seizure works only during the debtor's life.

stories.actor: Hama son of Rabba bar Abbahu
stories.event: Hama paid Avimi's debt in Bei Hozai and asked for the document.
stories.turn: The creditors said the money was for other debts.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu ruled that without witnesses he could not recover money or document.
stories.summary: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu sent payment through Hama, who paid and asked for the loan document. The creditors claimed the payment covered side debts. Rabbi Abbahu ruled that since Hama had no witnesses, the creditors were believed.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed with a bundle of rags
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags.
stories.turn: Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined whether it was worth a peruta.
stories.outcome: The betrothal depended on whether it had that value.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags. Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, sitting before Rav, examined it to see if it was worth a peruta, ruling the betrothal valid only if it was.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed with a blue marble stone, and his mother
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone and Rav Hisda assessed its value.
stories.turn: The man's mother claimed it had been worth a peruta on the day of betrothal.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda told her she could not make the woman forbidden to a later husband.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda estimated whether it was worth a peruta. The man's mother said it had been worth that much on the day. Rav Hisda answered that her word could not forbid the woman to someone else.

stories.actor: Yehudit, wife of Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Yehudit, suffering painful childbirths, told Rabbi Hiyya her mother said she had been betrothed to another as a child.
stories.turn: This claim would make her forbidden to him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hiyya said her mother had no power to forbid her to him.
stories.summary: Yehudit, Rabbi Hiyya's wife, had painful childbirths and wanted out of the marriage. She told him her mother said her father had accepted a betrothal for her when she was young. Rabbi Hiyya replied that her mother's word could not make her forbidden to him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: The Angel of Death was sent to do Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's bidding at his death, and he asked to see his place in paradise and to hold the knife.
stories.turn: At paradise he jumped in and swore not to return; God let the oath stand since he had never had an oath annulled.
stories.outcome: He was made to return the knife, Elijah announced him, and he met Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai in paradise.
stories.summary: As Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was dying, the Angel of Death was told to do his will. He asked to be shown his place in paradise and to hold the knife on the way, then leapt into paradise and swore not to leave. God ruled he could stay, a heavenly voice made him give back the knife, and Elijah proclaimed his arrival. Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai questioned him about rainbows in his day, and out of modesty he said one had been seen.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa
stories.event: When Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa was dying, he asked the Angel of Death for thirty days to review his learning, then for the knife.
stories.turn: The angel refused, suspecting a trick like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's.
stories.outcome: He died, a pillar of fire separated him from the world, and it withdrew only when Rabbi Alexandri asked in his own honor.
stories.summary: The Angel of Death, his friend, was sent to Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa, who asked for thirty days to review his studies. Afterward he asked to see his place and to hold the knife, but the angel refused, and dismissed his claim of fulfilling the whole Torah. When he died a pillar of fire surrounded him, and it lifted only when Rabbi Alexandri asked it to in his own honor.

stories.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: An Amorite asked how many kor of dates a palm on the Jordan bank yields, and was told sixty.
stories.turn: He mocked that the land had been ruined, since they used to pick 120.
stories.outcome: The resident replied that he meant only one side of the tree.
stories.summary: An Amorite asked a resident of Eretz Yisrael how much fruit a palm by the Jordan produced. Told sixty kor, he scoffed that they had ruined the land, since his people got 120. The resident answered that sixty was from one side only.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Rabbi Elazar ascended to Eretz Yisrael and was later ordained and seated in the intercalation council.
stories.turn: At each step he declared he had been spared another curse.
stories.outcome: By the third honor he said he had been spared three (continues past the window).
stories.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse. When ordained he said two, and when seated in the council that sets the calendar, three. The explanation continues beyond the window.

stories.actor: Ameimar
stories.event: While Ameimar judged, a man removed a feather from his head.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself from the case.
stories.summary: A feather landed on Ameimar's head while he sat in judgment, and a man removed it. Asked what he was doing there, the man said he had a case. Ameimar said he was disqualified from judging him.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: A man covered some spittle lying before Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man turned out to have a case before him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered spittle lying in front of Mar Ukva. When asked his business, he said he had a case. Mar Ukva declared himself unfit to judge it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the weekly fruit basket on Thursday instead of Friday.
stories.turn: He explained he had a case and brought it on the way.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael refused it, appointed other judges, and found himself still arguing for the man in his mind, and cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei's sharecropper usually brought fruit each Friday, but once came Thursday, saying he had a case that day. Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and disqualified himself, seating two scholars to judge. Pacing, he kept thinking of arguments for the sharecropper, and exclaimed that if he was so swayed without taking anything, how much more are those who take bribes.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha
stories.event: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing from a distant town.
stories.turn: He admitted he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael refused it and had others judge, yet still found himself biased, and cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, the first shearing, though there were priests closer to his town. He said he had a case and brought it on the way. Rabbi Yishmael refused, disqualified himself and appointed two scholars, but caught himself rehearsing the man's arguments and declared how much worse it must be for those who accept bribes.

stories.actor: Rav Anan
stories.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish and said he had a case.
stories.turn: Rav Anan refused, but the man said he wanted no judgment, only to give a gift like first fruits.
stories.outcome: Rav Anan accepted it and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note that he was disqualified (continues past the window).
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of fish, and when he mentioned a case Rav Anan refused it. The man said he no longer wanted Rav Anan's judgment, only to give a scholar a gift, which is like bringing first fruits. Rav Anan accepted and sent him to Rav Nahman saying he was disqualified; Rav Nahman assumed the man was a relative and began to defer an orphans' case.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son
stories.event: Rabbi arranged his son's marriage into the house of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: Seeing the bride, the son shortened it to six years, then married at once and was ashamed before his father.
stories.outcome: After twelve years' study his wife had become infertile; he prayed and she was healed.
stories.summary: A son was matched with a daughter of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's household, to study twelve years first. When she was shown to him he cut it to six, then decided to marry first, and was embarrassed before his father, who reassured him that God too moved up His plans. He then studied twelve years and returned to find his wife infertile; he prayed for her and she was cured.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai
stories.event: Rabbi Hananya left for twelve years of study and returned to find his town's paths changed.
stories.turn: He followed a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai' home, and his wife died of shock on seeing him.
stories.outcome: He prayed and she was revived.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and stayed twelve years. Returning, he could not find his house, but heard a girl called daughter of Hakhinai and followed her. His wife, sifting flour, looked up, saw him, and died from shock. He pleaded with God and she lived.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa
stories.event: After twelve years of study, Rabbi Hama sent word home rather than surprising his wife.
stories.turn: A sharp young scholar questioned him and he regretted not having such a son, not knowing it was his son Oshaya.
stories.outcome: At home he stood up for the young man, and his wife told him a father does not stand for his son.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa studied twelve years and, to avoid Ben Hakhinai's mistake, waited in the local study hall and sent word home. A brilliant young man questioned him, and he lamented that had he stayed home he might have such a son. When the young man followed him home and he rose in his honor, his wife asked whether a father stands for his son: it was his son Rabbi Oshaya.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter
stories.event: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter secretly betrothed herself to his shepherd Akiva on condition he study.
stories.turn: Her father expelled her and vowed she would not benefit from his property.
stories.outcome: Akiva studied twelve years and returned with twelve thousand students (story continues past the window).
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva was the shepherd of the wealthy Ben Kalba Savua, whose daughter saw his fine character and offered to marry him if he would study Torah. They betrothed secretly and she sent him off; her father threw her out and disinherited her. After twelve years Akiva returned with twelve thousand students and overheard an old man speaking to his wife; the story continues beyond the window.

stories.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
stories.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son to test him.
stories.turn: He wanted to see whether Rabba would grow angry.
stories.outcome: The Gemara explains he had waived his honor and tore at the seam.
stories.summary: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would become angry. The Gemara discusses whether this caused his son to stumble or wasted property, and explains that he had forgone his honor and tore only at a seam.

stories.actor: Rav Yehezkel and his sons
stories.event: Rav Yehezkel taught his son Rami a law about mixing condemned people.
stories.turn: His other son Rav Yehuda told him not to teach it that way and corrected the wording.
stories.outcome: Rav Yehuda proposed the reversed version (continues past the window).
stories.summary: Rav Yehezkel was teaching his son Rami that when those sentenced to burning are mixed with those sentenced to stoning, all are stoned. His other son Rav Yehuda objected, 'Father, do not teach it this way,' because majority alone would explain it. He offered the reversed wording instead.

stories.actor: The people of Bireta DeSatya
stories.event: A ditch overflowed with fish and the townspeople trapped them on Shabbat.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ahai son of Rabbi Yoshiya excommunicated them.
stories.outcome: They all abandoned Judaism, as Rabbi foresaw on his deathbed.
stories.summary: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declared that the people of Bireta DeSatya had that day turned from God. A ditch had overflowed with fish and they caught them on Shabbat. Rabbi Ahai son of Rabbi Yoshiya excommunicated them, and they apostatized.

stories.actor: Pelatiah son of Benaiah
stories.event: Nebuchadnezzar's son-in-law asked for captives to serve him, and Nebuchadnezzar planned to send Jews.
stories.turn: Pelatiah advised Nebuchadnezzar to keep the nobles himself and send the servants instead.
stories.outcome: Ezekiel lamented that one who did good for Israel should die in mid-life.
stories.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's son-in-law, governor of Meishan, complained he had been sent no captives to serve him. Nebuchadnezzar meant to send Jews, but Pelatiah son of Benaiah suggested the important Jews stay to serve the king and their slaves go instead. When Pelatiah died, Ezekiel cried out that one who did Israel this good should die halfway through his days.

stories.actor: A man who sold land to Rav Pappa
stories.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money to buy oxen.
stories.turn: In the end he did not need the money.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land to him, beyond the letter of the law.
stories.summary: A man sold land to Rav Pappa to raise money for oxen. When it turned out he did not need the money, Rav Pappa gave him back his land, going beyond what the law required.

stories.actor: The people of Neharde'a and Rav Nahman
stories.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
stories.turn: Wheat then arrived and the sales proved unnecessary.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions return to their owners.
stories.summary: In a drought in Neharde'a, everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat. Then wheat arrived. Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions go back to their original owners.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda, Sumakhos, and Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: After Rabbi Meir's death, Rabbi Yehuda barred Rabbi Meir's students from his study hall, but Sumakhos pushed in and quoted a ruling of Rabbi Meir.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yehuda became angry and dismissed the ruling as irrelevant, since a woman would not be in the Temple courtyard.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yosei spoke up, refusing to stay silent, and showed the ruling was relevant.
stories.summary: After Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda told his students not to let Rabbi Meir's quarrelsome students in. Sumakhos forced his way in and cited a ruling from Rabbi Meir about betrothal with a priest's portion. Rabbi Yehuda angrily dismissed it as pointless, but Rabbi Yosei said he would not let the Torah suffer through silence and explained cases where the ruling matters.

stories.actor: A man who sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: A man sold his property intending to move to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: He went but could not settle there, and sought to cancel the sale.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the sale could be nullified (another version: that it could not).
stories.summary: A man sold his property in order to move to Eretz Yisrael. He went but was unable to settle, and on returning wanted to undo the sale. Rava ruled that since he went intending to settle and failed, he could cancel it; another version reports the opposite ruling.

stories.actor: Another man who sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: A man sold his property intending to move to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: In the end he did not go.
stories.outcome: Rav Ashi ruled that he could have gone had he wished, so the sale stands.
stories.summary: Another man sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael but never went. Rav Ashi ruled that going was in his own hands, so he could not cancel the sale.

stories.actor: A daughter left a palm tree in her father's will
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter.
stories.turn: The heirs divided the estate and gave her no tree at all.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled they must give her a tree and redivide the estate.
stories.summary: A man left instructions that his daughter receive a palm tree. The heirs divided the property and gave her nothing, each implying it was in another's share. Rav Yosef compared it to the mishna, but Abaye ruled the heirs must give her a tree and divide the estate afresh.

stories.actor: A second daughter left a palm tree
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter but died leaving only two half-shares of palm trees.
stories.turn: The heirs wanted to give her the two halves, and Rav Ashi questioned whether that counts as a palm tree.
stories.outcome: Rav Mordekhai reported Rava's view that two halves count as a palm tree.
stories.summary: A man left his daughter a palm tree but owned only halves of two trees. The heirs offered her the two halves. Rav Ashi was unsure if that fulfilled the will, and Rav Mordekhai told him, in Rava's name, that people do call two halves a palm tree.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya bar Adda and Reish Lakish
stories.event: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, a schoolteacher, was absent three days harvesting a vine his father left him.
stories.turn: The vine's yield dropped each day.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish told him the yield would have been greater had he not neglected the children's Torah study.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, who taught children for Reish Lakish, missed three days of teaching. He explained he was harvesting an enormously fruitful vine, though its yield fell each day. Reish Lakish told him the vine would have produced even more had he not left his teaching.

stories.actor: Rami bar Yehezkel
stories.event: Rami bar Yehezkel came to Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under fig trees.
stories.turn: Honey dripped from the figs and milk from the goats, mixing together.
stories.outcome: He declared this is what 'flowing with milk and honey' means.
stories.summary: Visiting Benei Berak, Rami bar Yehezkel saw goats under fig trees, with honey dripping from the figs and milk from the goats mingling on the ground. He said this was the meaning of a land flowing with milk and honey.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina
stories.event: Three Sages visiting a place were served a peach as large as a five-se'a stewpot.
stories.turn: The peach was too big to finish.
stories.outcome: They ate a third, declared a third ownerless, and gave a third to their animals.
stories.summary: Three Sages came to a certain place and were served a peach the size of a large stewpot. They ate one third, left one third ownerless, and fed the last third to their animals.

stories.actor: The daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon
stories.event: The Sages allotted her two se'a of wine a week for pudding from her husband's estate.
stories.turn: She blessed them that they should allot the same to their own daughters.
stories.outcome: Since she was a widow awaiting levirate marriage, they did not answer amen.
stories.summary: After her husband died, the Sages allotted Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter-in-law a large weekly portion of wine. She blessed them that their daughters should receive the same. Because she was a widow awaiting her yavam, they did not answer amen.

stories.actor: Homa, Abaye's widow, Rava, and Rava's wife
stories.event: Homa asked Rava for sustenance and wine; while showing the size of Abaye's cups her arm was exposed.
stories.turn: Her beauty lit up the court, and Rava went home aroused; his wife learned who had been there.
stories.outcome: Rava's wife beat Homa with a chest lock and drove her out of Mehoza.
stories.summary: Abaye's widow Homa came to Rava for support and asked for wine, claiming Abaye gave her large cups of it. As she gestured, her arm was uncovered and her beauty lit the courtroom. Rava went home and approached his wife, who discovered why, chased Homa out of town beating her, and accused her of having killed three husbands and coming for a fourth.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava
stories.event: She asked Rav Nehemya for sustenance and wine.
stories.turn: He considered whether she was entitled to wine.
stories.outcome: He granted it because the people of Mehoza drink wine.
stories.summary: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rava asked Rav Nehemya to set her sustenance and wine. He granted both, explaining that the people of Mehoza customarily drink wine.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
stories.event: She asked Rav Yosef for sustenance, wine, and silk garments.
stories.turn: He asked why she needed silk.
stories.outcome: She answered: for you, your friends, and your friends' friends.
stories.summary: A widow came before Rav Yosef and asked for sustenance and wine, which he granted. When she also asked for silk and he asked why, she replied that it was so she would not be shamed before him and his colleagues.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a girl with vegetables
stories.event: A man betrothed a minor girl, without her father's consent, with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace.
stories.turn: The question arose whether the father might have approved.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled there was no concern because the betrothal was degrading.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a minor girl in the marketplace with a bundle of vegetables. Ravina ruled that because this was a degrading way to betroth, there was no concern that the father had approved. Asked which part was degrading, he said both.

stories.actor: A father, mother, and the father's relative
stories.event: Parents disputed which relative their daughter should marry, and the father gave in to the mother.
stories.turn: During the betrothal meal, the father's relative climbed to the roof and betrothed her himself.
stories.outcome: The Sages ruled the father did not want that betrothal.
stories.summary: A father wanted his daughter to marry his relative, the mother wanted hers, and he finally gave in. While everyone ate at the betrothal feast, the father's relative went up to the roof and betrothed the girl. Abaye and Rava gave reasons why the father is presumed not to have wanted this.

stories.actor: The Elders of Nezonya, Rav Hamnuna and Rav Hisda
stories.event: The Elders of Nezonya skipped Rav Hisda's lecture, and he sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them.
stories.turn: They posed Rav Hamnuna a question he could not answer and mocked his name.
stories.outcome: Rav Hamnuna returned to Rav Hisda, who showed him the answer was in a baraita.
stories.summary: When the Elders of Nezonya stayed away from his lecture, Rav Hisda sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them. They said Rav Hisda had not answered their question, and when Rav Hamnuna invited them to ask him instead, he could not answer either, so they mocked him as 'Karnuna'. He went back to Rav Hisda, who told him the answer was in a known baraita.

stories.actor: Rav Amram the Pious
stories.event: Redeemed captive women were lodged in Rav Amram's attic, and seeing one's beauty he lifted a huge ladder and began to climb.
stories.turn: Halfway up he stopped himself and shouted 'Fire in Amram's house!'
stories.outcome: He drove out his evil inclination, which left him like a pillar of fire, and told it he was superior to it.
stories.summary: Captive women were brought to Rav Amram's house and the ladder was removed. Seeing one of them, he lifted a ladder ten men could not lift and started up. Halfway, he braced himself and cried 'fire', summoning the Sages; when they said he had shamed them, he said better shame now than in the World-to-Come, and he expelled his evil inclination as a pillar of fire.

stories.actor: Rabbi Meir
stories.event: Rabbi Meir mocked sinners, and Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river.
stories.turn: He began crossing a rope bridge after her.
stories.outcome: Halfway across Satan left him, saying only heaven's warning about him had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared as a woman on the far bank, and Rabbi Meir started across a rope bridge toward her. Halfway, Satan let go and said that only the heavenly proclamation protecting him had kept him from ruin.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva
stories.event: Rabbi Akiva mocked sinners, and Satan appeared to him as a woman atop a palm tree.
stories.turn: He began climbing the tree.
stories.outcome: Halfway up Satan left him, saying only heaven's warning about him had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also scoffed at sinners. Satan appeared as a woman at the top of a palm tree and Rabbi Akiva began to climb. Halfway up Satan let go, saying only the heavenly proclamation had saved him.

stories.actor: Peleimu
stories.event: Peleimu daily taunted Satan, who came to him on Yom Kippur eve as a repulsive pauper and was seated at his table.
stories.turn: The pauper spat in a cup, was rebuked, and pretended to die, so people said Peleimu killed a man.
stories.outcome: Satan revealed himself to the hiding Peleimu and told him to say 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan' instead.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to say 'an arrow in Satan's eye' every day. On Yom Kippur eve Satan came as a sore-covered beggar, demanded to eat inside at the table, behaved disgustingly, then collapsed as if dead, and people cried that Peleimu had killed him. Peleimu hid in the outhouse; Satan followed, revealed himself, and told him to change his taunt to a prayer that God rebuke Satan.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi and his wife
stories.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi always prayed to be saved from the evil inclination.
stories.turn: His wife overheard and wondered why, since he had abstained from her for years.
stories.outcome: The window ends before the outcome.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi prayed daily to be saved from the evil inclination. His wife heard him and wondered why, since he had withdrawn from her for years because of his age. The story continues past the window.

stories.actor: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi
stories.event: Two rabbis studying Torah stood up when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed.
stories.turn: He objected that they were ordained and he was not, and that Torah need not stand for its students.
stories.outcome: He told them they need not have stood.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi were studying when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba walked by, and they rose for him. He told them they need not have, since they were ordained and he was only an associate, and since those studying Torah need not rise for its scholars.

stories.actor: Rav Ika bar Avin, Abaye and Rav Hananel
stories.event: Rav Ika bar Avin reported in Rav's name that Hillazon Nihavnad has unflawed lineage.
stories.turn: Abaye accused him of bias, since a yevama from there had fallen to him.
stories.outcome: They asked Rav Hananel, who confirmed the ruling was Rav's.
stories.summary: Rav Ika bar Avin taught that Hillazon Nihavnad has unflawed lineage. Abaye told people to ignore him, since he had a personal interest in a widow from there. Rav Ika said the ruling came from Rav Hananel, and when they asked, Rav Hananel confirmed it.

stories.actor: Rav Ashi, Mar Zutra and the king's butler
stories.event: Seeing Mar Zutra grow pale with craving as the king's food passed, Rav Ashi put some in his mouth.
stories.turn: The butler said he spoiled the king's meal; Rav Ashi said the meat was diseased and pointed to the exact spot.
stories.outcome: They found the leprous defect, and Rav Ashi explained he had seen a leprous spirit over it.
stories.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat at King Izgur's gate as his butler carried food by. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra blanch with craving and put some food in his mouth. Accused of ruining the king's meal, he claimed the meat was leprous; when nothing was found, he pointed to a spot where it was found, explaining he had seen a leprous spirit hovering over it.

stories.actor: A Roman and a woman
stories.event: A Roman proposed to a woman who refused, so he ate pomegranates before her without sharing until she became ill.
stories.turn: He offered to cure her if she would marry him, and she agreed.
stories.outcome: He had her spit out her saliva while he ate pomegranates, a green leaf-like thing came out, and she was cured.
stories.summary: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she said no. He ate pomegranates in front of her, giving her none, until swallowing her craving made her ill. He then offered to cure her if she married him; she agreed, and by spitting out her saliva as he ate she expelled something like a green leaf and recovered.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva, his wife, and ben Kalba Savua
stories.event: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter betrothed herself to his shepherd Akiva on condition he study, and her father disinherited her.
stories.turn: Akiva studied 24 years and returned with 24,000 students; his wife was recognized, and her father came seeking release from his vow.
stories.outcome: Akiva revealed who he was, and ben Kalba Savua bowed to him and gave him half his wealth.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva was ben Kalba Savua's shepherd; the rich man's daughter secretly married him on condition he go study, and her father threw her out and vowed she would get nothing. Akiva studied twelve years, overheard her urging him to stay longer, and studied twelve more, returning with 24,000 students; he honored her before them, saying all their Torah was hers. Her father came to have his vow annulled, said he would never have vowed had he known Akiva would learn even a little, and when Akiva revealed himself he fell at his feet and gave him half his fortune.

stories.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rava and his father
stories.event: Rav Yosef son of Rava, sent to study for six years, left after three to visit his wife on Yom Kippur eve.
stories.turn: His father came out to meet him with a weapon and rebuked him.
stories.outcome: Both were so caught up in the argument that neither ate the pre-fast meal.
stories.summary: Rava sent his son to study with Rav Yosef for six years. After three, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the son set out to visit his wife. Rava met him armed and rebuked him for remembering his wife, and in the quarrel neither ate the meal before the fast.

stories.actor: Disputing heirs and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A Sage threatened heirs with excommunication unless they appeased the others and sent them to Rav Nahman.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman considered the change in the estate's value.
stories.outcome: He ruled the heirs acquired rights according to the estate's value at the father's death.
stories.summary: Picking up mid-story, a Sage warned some heirs he would excommunicate them if they did not appease the others, then sent them to Rav Nahman. Rav Nahman ruled that, just as with depreciated property, when property appreciated the heirs' rights are fixed at the time of the father's death.

stories.actor: A purchaser of two mansions and a creditor
stories.event: A debtor sold two mansions; his creditor seized one and then sought the other.
stories.turn: The purchaser offered: accept the first as full payment, or take 1,000 dinars and leave both.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the creditor must accept, since he loses nothing.
stories.summary: A man owing 1,000 dinars sold his two mansions for 500 each. The creditor seized one, then came for the other. The buyer offered him either to accept the first as full payment or take 1,000 dinars and release both; Rami bar Hama compared it to the mishna, but Rava ruled the creditor loses nothing and should accept.

stories.actor: A purchaser of two plots and a creditor
stories.event: A debtor sold two plots; his creditor seized one and then sought the other.
stories.turn: The purchaser offered: accept the first as full payment, or take 100 dinars and leave both.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled the creditor must accept, since he loses nothing.
stories.summary: A man owing 100 dinars sold two small plots for 50 each. The creditor seized one and came for the other. The buyer offered the same choice; Rav Yosef compared it to the mishna, but Abaye ruled the creditor loses nothing and should accept.

stories.actor: Two men drinking wine in Babylonia
stories.event: One man gave the other a cup of wine as betrothal of the other's daughter to his son.
stories.turn: The question arose whether the son had consented.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled no betrothal: we do not assume the son agreed.
stories.summary: Two men were drinking under poplar trees in Babylonia, and one handed the other a cup of wine to betroth the other's daughter to his son. Ravina ruled that we do not assume the son approved, and he rejected the Sages' suggestions that the son had appointed his father or made his wishes known.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a girl with vegetables
stories.event: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace.
stories.turn: The question arose whether the father might have approved.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled there was no concern because the betrothal was degrading.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a minor girl in the marketplace with a bundle of vegetables. Ravina ruled that because this was degrading, there was no concern that the father had approved, and said both the vegetables and the marketplace made it degrading.

stories.actor: A father, mother, and the father's relative
stories.event: Parents disputed which relative their daughter should marry, and the father gave in to the mother.
stories.turn: During the betrothal meal, the father's relative climbed to the roof and betrothed her himself.
stories.outcome: The Sages ruled the father did not want that betrothal.
stories.summary: A father wanted his daughter to marry his relative, the mother wanted hers, and he finally gave in. During the feast the father's relative went up to the roof and betrothed her. Abaye and Rava gave reasons why the father is presumed not to have wanted it.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride, and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom complained he found no blood, while the bride insisted she was a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel had the cloth soaked and laundered and found drops of blood.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to go take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi saying he found no blood on his wedding night; his bride said she had been a virgin. Rabban Gamliel had the cloth soaked and washed and found drops of blood. He told the groom his bride was a virgin.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride, and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom complained he found no blood, while the bride insisted she was still a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel tested two maidservants on a wine barrel, then tested the bride, and no wine scent came from her.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to go take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: Another groom said he found no blood and his bride said she was still a virgin. Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi seated a virgin and a non-virgin maidservant on a wine barrel and found the wine's scent came only from the non-virgin. When the bride was tested, no scent came, and he told the groom she was a virgin.

stories.actor: A woman, her brothers, and Ameimar
stories.event: A woman came before Ameimar claiming a tenth of her father's estate.
stories.turn: Her brothers said they would pay her off in cash if they had the money.
stories.outcome: Ameimar stayed silent, showing he agreed they could pay her in money.
stories.summary: Rav Minyumi was with Ameimar when a woman came claiming a tenth of her father's estate for her dowry. Her brothers told her they would buy her out with money if they had it. Ameimar said nothing, which Rav Minyumi took to mean he accepted that she could be paid off in cash.

stories.actor: Rav Anan, Rav Huna, Rav Sheshet and Mar Ukva
stories.event: Rav Anan wrote to Rav Huna, addressing him as 'our friend', instructing him to give a woman a tenth of the estate.
stories.turn: Rav Huna, offended, sent back a sharp reply via Rav Sheshet: 'Anan, Anan... who sits at the head of the marzeiha?'
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva told Rav Anan he had been wrong to address Rav Huna as a peer when he did not even know what marzeiha meant.
stories.summary: Rav Anan sent Rav Huna a letter calling him 'Huna our friend' and telling him to give a woman her dowry share. Rav Huna made Rav Sheshet, on pain of excommunication, deliver a curt reply mocking Rav Anan. Rav Anan, puzzled and hurt, consulted Mar Ukva, who told him that someone who did not know what marzeiha (mourner) meant had no business calling Rav Huna his friend.

stories.actor: Mar Zutra and a rebellious wife
stories.event: A woman refused her husband, saying he disgusted her.
stories.turn: Mar Zutra compelled her to stay with him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hanina of Sura was born of the couple, though the Gemara attributes this to heavenly help.
stories.summary: A woman rebelled against her husband, saying he disgusted her, and Mar Zutra forced her to remain married. From that couple came Rabbi Hanina of Sura. The Gemara says this was heavenly assistance and not a precedent.

stories.actor: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law and Rav Gamda
stories.event: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled while holding a garment, and Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi ruled on her worn clothes.
stories.turn: Rav Gamda accused them of bending the law out of regard for Rav Zevid, since Rava left the question unresolved.
stories.outcome: The ruling became: what she seized is not taken from her; what she did not seize is not given.
stories.summary: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband while holding a garment. Three Sages ruled on whether she lost her worn clothes, and Rav Gamda accused them of flattering (or, in another version, bending the law against) the great Rav Zevid, since Rava had left it open. The outcome: she keeps what she holds and gets nothing more.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tarfon and his mother
stories.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could step on him getting in and out of bed.
stories.turn: He boasted of it in the study hall.
stories.outcome: They told him he had not reached half the honor due her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would bend down so his mother could climb onto and off her bed by stepping on him. When he boasted of this in the study hall, the Sages told him he had not reached half of what honoring her requires, asking whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea without him shaming her.

stories.actor: Rav Asi and his elderly mother
stories.event: Rav Asi's senile mother made escalating demands, including a husband as handsome as him, so he left for Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: Hearing she was following him, he got Rabbi Yohanan's blessing to leave the land to meet her.
stories.outcome: On the way he learned her coffin was arriving and said had he known, he would not have left.
stories.summary: Rav Asi's aged mother demanded jewelry and then a husband as handsome as her son, so he left for Eretz Yisrael. When he heard she was following, he asked Rabbi Yohanan about leaving the land to meet her and received an ambiguous blessing, which Rabbi Elazar assured him was permission. Meanwhile he heard that her coffin was on its way and said that had he known, he would not have gone out.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son
stories.event: He went to study for twelve years after his wedding.
stories.turn: On his return his wife had become infertile, and divorce or a second wife would both shame her.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she was cured.
stories.summary: Rabbi's son left to study for twelve years and came back to find his wife infertile. Rabbi saw that divorcing her or taking a second wife would both humiliate her, so the husband prayed for mercy and she was healed.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai
stories.event: He left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and studied for twelve years.
stories.turn: On returning he could not find his home; when his wife saw him she died from shock.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she was revived.
stories.summary: Hananya ben Hakhinai went off to study for twelve years. When he returned the town had changed; he found his house by following a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai'. His wife saw him suddenly and died of shock, and after he protested to God and prayed, she lived.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa
stories.event: After twelve years of study he went to the local study hall first and sent word home.
stories.turn: He met a brilliant young scholar, not realizing it was his own son, and later stood up for him at home.
stories.outcome: His wife pointed out that a father was standing for his son.
stories.summary: Hama bar Bisa, wishing to avoid Ben Hakhinai's mistake, sent word home before arriving. In the study hall he was impressed by a sharp young man and regretted not having such a son; at home he rose for the same young man, and his wife told him it was his son Oshaya.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter
stories.event: She betrothed herself to the shepherd Akiva on condition he study, and her father disinherited her.
stories.turn: Akiva returned after twenty-four years with thousands of students, honored his wife, and her father came to annul his vow.
stories.outcome: Akiva revealed himself; the father kissed his feet and gave him half his wealth.
stories.summary: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter married the shepherd Akiva secretly and sent him to study, and her father cast her out. Akiva studied twelve years, overheard her urging another twelve, and returned with 24,000 students; he defended her when his attendants pushed her away. Her father came to the great sage to annul his vow, learned the sage was Akiva, and gave him half his property.

stories.actor: A Madonite in Jerusalem
stories.event: Wishing to give away his movable property, he was told it must be transferred by means of land.
stories.turn: He bought a small plot near Jerusalem and gave the property along with portions of it.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages carried out his gift.
stories.summary: A Madonite in Jerusalem wanted to give away his many movables and was told he could only do so through land. He acquired a plot, gave its northern part with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, then died, and the Sages upheld his gift.

stories.actor: A man in Jerusalem
stories.event: He wanted to give his movables as a gift and was told to do it through land.
stories.turn: He bought a small plot and gave a handbreadth of it with sheep and barrels.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages fulfilled his words.
stories.summary: A man in Jerusalem, sick or healthy depending on the version, wished to give away his movable property. Told it had to go through land, he bought a beit rova and gave a square handbreadth with a hundred sheep and barrels. He died and the Sages carried out his instructions.

stories.actor: Ulla and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Ulla, who often went up to Eretz Yisrael, died abroad.
stories.turn: Told his coffin was being brought to the Land, Rabbi Elazar said burial after death is not like being received alive.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Elazar lamented him despite the coffin's return.
stories.summary: Ulla died outside Eretz Yisrael and Rabbi Elazar lamented that he died in an unclean land. When told his coffin was coming, he replied that being absorbed by the Land in life is not like after death.

stories.actor: A man with a yevama in Bei Hoza'a
stories.event: He asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go down to Babylonia to perform levirate marriage.
stories.turn: Rabbi Hanina said his brother had left and died for it.
stories.outcome: He told him not to follow his brother out of the Land.
stories.summary: A man in Eretz Yisrael whose brother's widow lived in Babylonia asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go there to marry her. Rabbi Hanina answered that his brother had married abroad and God killed him, so why should he follow?

stories.actor: A man who left Pumbedita for Bei Kuvei
stories.event: He moved from Pumbedita to Bei Kuvei.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef held this forbidden.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef excommunicated him.
stories.summary: A man left Pumbedita to live in Bei Kuvei, beyond Babylonia proper, and Rav Yosef excommunicated him.

stories.actor: A scholar who left Pumbedita for Astonia
stories.event: He moved from Pumbedita to Astonia.
stories.turn: He died there.
stories.outcome: Abaye said he would have lived had he stayed.
stories.summary: A Torah scholar left Pumbedita for Astonia and died. Abaye remarked that had he wished to stay in Babylonia he would still be alive.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Rabbi Hiyya visited the ill Rabbi and found him crying.
stories.turn: Hiyya reminded him that dying in tears is a bad sign.
stories.outcome: Rabbi explained he was crying for the Torah and mitzvot he would lose.
stories.summary: When Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya came in and found him weeping, and asked why, since crying at death is an ill omen. Rabbi answered that he wept for the Torah and commandments he could no longer fulfill.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: During an argument Hanina boasted he could restore the Torah by his analysis if it were forgotten.
stories.turn: Hiyya answered that he works so it will never be forgotten.
stories.outcome: Hiyya described planting flax, hunting deer, making scrolls and teaching children who teach each other.
stories.summary: Arguing with Rabbi Hiyya, Rabbi Hanina claimed he could rebuild a forgotten Torah through his reasoning.
